The docs directory contains top-level project documentation covering App Store compliance requirements, content licensing terms, a project README, a device setup guide, and Apple Watch testing procedures. It also includes a knowledge bowl validation test vectors file that defines expected behavior for the Quiz Bowl feature. Although it has no direct code dependencies, it is consulted throughout the development and release process to ensure regulatory, quality, and onboarding standards are met. Contributors setting up a new device or preparing a submission to the App Store should start here.

This documentation collection covers all iOS-specific engineering guidance for UnaMentis, including coding style, module authoring patterns, best practice reviews, and deep research audits of on-device LLM and STT options evaluated through mid-2026. It includes a Rust/Candle pathway investigation for the Kyutai Pocket model and a July 2026 module architecture analysis. Rules embedded in the files document audio threshold decisions, visual asset type handling, and image loading phase policies that directly inform how the Core Audio and Context modules are built. Reviewers should consult this directory before making changes to on-device inference, audio processing thresholds, or module structure.

This directory holds the project's testing strategy documentation, covering AI simulator testing procedures, CI integration test triage guidance, coverage campaign goals, a debug testing UI reference, knowledge bowl validation testing steps, a QA coverage audit report, and a QA pipeline fix log from June 2026. It is the authoritative reference for understanding how the test suite is structured, which areas have coverage gaps, and how to reproduce CI failures. The 7 files in this directory collectively constitute the testing knowledge base rather than executable test code. Contributors diagnosing CI failures or planning new test coverage should start here.

The root component represents the unamentis-ios application itself, an AI-powered educational iOS client built with SwiftUI. It serves as the top-level container that owns all modules, screens, and services within the project. With 17 files and 1735 lines at the root level, it holds project configuration files including linting rules, contribution guides, and agent instructions. CI tests are configured at this level, enforcing an 80% coverage threshold and managing topic domain policy across twelve subject areas including science, mathematics, literature, and history.

The scripts directory provides the project's developer automation tooling, including multiple Python scripts for adding source files, frameworks, and test files to the Xcode project file, along with shell scripts for code formatting, health checks, hook audits, and feature flag audits. These automate repetitive Xcode project management tasks that would otherwise require error-prone manual edits to the .pbxproj file. The add-to-xcode scripts expose a command interface supporting operations such as add-files, add-source, add-framework, list-files, and verify. They are invoked by developers during module setup and CI bootstrapping, not at runtime.

WatchModels is a shared data-model module defining the communication contract between the iOS app and an Apple Watch companion. It contains two files: SessionCommand, which enumerates watch-originating control signals (pause, resume, mute, unmute, stop), and WatchSessionState, which tracks session progress as a ratio of completed to total segments. Because it sits in a Shared directory, both the iOS and watchOS targets can import it without duplication. No edges connect to it from the analyzed graph, but its role as a shared contract makes it load-bearing for any Watch integration.

UnaMentis is the root iOS client module built on UIKit, serving as the top-level application container that hosts all screens, services, and business logic for the AI-powered tutoring platform. It receives 32 inbound edges from the rest of the architecture, making it the terminal aggregation point where all UI screens, background services, and data flows converge. The module tracks real-time performance metrics including per-endpoint latency, memory utilization percentages, and conversation interruption rates, and enforces thermal state policies across four severity levels (nominal, fair, serious, critical). It manages feature gating for capabilities including LLM validation, custom dictionaries, advanced analytics, and offline mode, with OpenAI integration driving the AI tutoring capability at the core. The complete absence of test files despite CI infrastructure in place represents a significant quality risk for a module of this size and complexity.

The UnaMentis Watch App is the Apple Watch companion target for the UnaMentis iOS application, providing a watchOS-native entry point for study and session features. Built as a thin SwiftUI shell, it bootstraps the watch UI and connects to the paired iPhone via WatchConnectivity. It reaches outward to the root project for shared configuration and to the main UnaMentis iOS target for runtime data exchange. As the sole executable target on the watch platform, it is the gateway through which all watch-side user interactions flow.

Active Session is a watchOS SwiftUI screen that displays the real-time state of an ongoing study or exercise session on the user's wrist. With no detected inbound or outbound navigation edges it is likely presented programmatically or modally rather than through a standard NavigationLink. At 78 lines it is a compact, focused view almost certainly rendering a timer, progress indicator, or live feedback from an in-progress session. It serves as the primary glanceable display for the watch user while a session is running.

KBWatch Domain Drill is a watchOS SwiftUI screen that presents focused practice questions scoped to a single Knowledge Bowl domain, allowing the user to target a specific subject area. It receives navigation exclusively from KBWatch Main and has no further outbound navigation, making it a terminal study destination. At 232 lines it contains substantial UI logic for presenting questions and capturing answers within the constrained watchOS environment. Users land here when they want deliberate, domain-specific repetition rather than a mixed session.

KBWatch Flash Cards is a watchOS SwiftUI screen that presents Knowledge Bowl content in a flip-card study format directly on the Apple Watch. It is navigated to from KBWatch Main and has no further outbound navigation, functioning as a terminal review surface. At 278 lines it is the largest individual KB watch screen, reflecting the complexity of managing card state, flip animation, and correctness tracking within watchOS constraints. Users swipe or tap through cards to build recall of Knowledge Bowl material.

KBWatch Main is the hub screen for the Knowledge Bowl section of the UnaMentis Watch App, serving as the navigation root for all watch-side KB study modes. It branches to three distinct destinations: Domain Drill, Flash Cards, and Quick Session, covering every KB practice format available on the watch. With 3 outbound navigation edges and 0 inbound edges it is an entry point into the KB feature tree rather than a destination. At 163 lines it functions primarily as a mode-selection menu that routes the user to their preferred study format.

KBWatch Quick Session is a watchOS SwiftUI screen that runs a rapid, time-boxed Knowledge Bowl practice session directly on the Apple Watch without additional configuration. It is reached from KBWatch Main and has no further navigation targets, functioning as a self-contained quiz runner from start through results. At 314 lines it is the most complex of the KB watch screens, managing question sequencing, timing, per-question scoring, and a session summary within a single view lifecycle. It provides the fastest path from wrist raise to active Knowledge Bowl practice.

The Services module provides the two core system-level services that underpin the UnaMentis Watch App: ExtendedRuntimeManager requests and manages watchOS extended runtime sessions to keep the app alive during active use, and WatchConnectivityService bridges bidirectional communication with the paired iPhone using the WatchConnectivity framework. It encodes an explicit policy for handling extended runtime termination reasons, covering session-in-progress, expiry, resigned-frontmost, error, and system-suppression cases. Without this module the watch app cannot maintain a live session past the standard foreground window or exchange data with the iOS side.

The Views module groups the three top-level watchOS UI screens shared across the watch app: ContentView (the root container), IdleView (displayed when no session is active), and ActiveSessionView (displayed during a live session). These files form the primary display surface a user sees on app launch and between study sessions. No detected navigation edges suggest their presentation is driven programmatically by app state rather than through NavigationLink. At 187 lines across three files it is a lean, focused layer that switches between idle and active states.

The Components module contains reusable watchOS UI primitives shared across the watch app's views: ControlButtonsView provides tap targets for session control actions such as pause and stop, and ProgressRingView renders a circular progress indicator. These building blocks are composed into larger screens but have no detected navigation relationships of their own. At 107 lines across two files they are compact, single-purpose components whose visual consistency is relied upon by every screen that embeds them.

The KnowledgeBowl views module is the largest UI cluster in the Watch App, collecting all four Knowledge Bowl screens: Main, Domain Drill, Flash Cards, and Quick Session. It encodes two notable business rules: accuracy is computed as correct answers divided by total questions, and session mode switches between missed-questions review and random question order. At 987 lines across four files it represents the dominant feature surface on the watch. Navigation edges are tracked at the individual screen level, so this module boundary shows no edges of its own.

Active Todo List is a SwiftUI screen that displays the subset of todo items currently in an active (incomplete, non-archived) state. It shares its implementation file with the Archived and Completed variants, suggesting a filtered view pattern where a single view file drives multiple list modes. As a leaf screen with no recorded inbound or outbound navigation edges, it is likely embedded within a tab or parent container rather than navigated to explicitly. It gives users their primary working view of pending tasks.

The Analytics screen presents aggregated performance and usage statistics for the user's study sessions within UnaMentis. It is reached via the More tab and serves as the primary destination for reviewing progress over time. The view renders charts, session breakdowns, and trend data drawn from locally stored session records. It has no outbound navigation, making it a leaf destination in the app's flow.

The APIProvider Detail screen shows configuration and runtime statistics for a specific AI API provider such as an OpenAI-compatible endpoint or a Claude backend. It is navigated to from Settings when a user selects a provider entry from the list. The view exposes per-provider settings including API keys, model selection, and rate limits. It is a leaf screen with no further outbound navigation.

Archived Todo List is a SwiftUI screen that presents todo items the user has explicitly archived rather than completed or deleted. It shares its implementation file with the Active and Completed list variants, indicating a multi-mode list view architecture. With no recorded navigation edges it is likely a tab-embedded or conditionally displayed surface. It lets users review and potentially restore previously archived work.

The Audio Recorder screen provides the voice capture interface used during voice cloning setup. It is presented as a modal sheet from the Chatterbox Settings screen, allowing users to record voice samples that will be used to synthesize a personalized voice. The screen is a leaf in the navigation graph with no outbound transitions, meaning it captures audio and returns control to its presenter. Its placement in VoiceCloningViews.swift confirms it is dedicated to the voice cloning enrollment flow.

The Audio Test screen lets users verify microphone input and speaker output in isolation before relying on them during a live session. It is accessed from the Settings hub as a diagnostic aid for troubleshooting audio hardware or permission issues. The screen captures a short audio sample, plays it back, and surfaces any device-level audio permission or hardware problems. It has no outbound navigation and is a leaf within the settings flow.

Aural Drill Session is the active practice screen for ear-training exercises within the Aural Skills module. It is reached via navigation from the Aural Skills Dashboard and presents an interactive drill interface where the learner responds to audio stimuli. The screen lives alongside the dashboard in AuralSkillsViews.swift, sharing 309 lines of SwiftUI view code between the two screens. As a leaf screen with one inbound edge and no outbound edges, it is the terminal destination for the aural skills flow.

Aural Skills Dashboard is the entry point for the ear-training feature area, providing an overview of available drills and the learner's progress in musical or auditory skills. It navigates forward to the Aural Drill Session screen when the user selects a practice activity. The view is colocated with the drill session in a single 309-line SwiftUI file. With one outbound navigation edge and no inbound edges, it acts as the hub screen for its feature area.

The Barge-In Tuning screen provides controls for adjusting the sensitivity threshold at which the user's voice interrupts ongoing TTS playback. It is reached from Settings and allows fine-grained tuning to reduce false positives or missed interruptions in hands-free mode. At 110 lines it is a focused, single-purpose configuration screen. It has no outbound navigation.

Chatterbox Settings is a dedicated configuration screen for the Chatterbox feature, reachable via a NavigationLink from the Voice Settings screen. It exposes controls specific to Chatterbox behavior and hosts the entry point for voice cloning enrollment by presenting the Audio Recorder as a modal sheet. With one inbound navigation edge and one outbound modal edge, it acts as a mid-level settings node sitting between the broader Voice Settings hub and the voice recording flow. Changes made here affect how the Chatterbox synthesizes or delivers speech.

Completed Todo List is a SwiftUI screen showing todo items the user has marked done. It shares its implementation file with the Active and Archived variants, reflecting a unified list view parameterized by completion state. No navigation edges are recorded, placing it likely as a tab-level or segmented-control-driven surface. It provides a historical record of accomplished tasks.

Curriculum Detail presents a single curriculum item in full, giving users the ability to inspect its content, structure, and available topics before deciding to engage with it. It is navigated to from the Curriculum list screen via a sheet presentation and is the only known inbound entry point. From here, users can drill further into individual topics by opening the Topic Detail sheet, making this screen the middle tier of the three-level curriculum browsing hierarchy. It is essential for connecting the high-level curriculum catalog to the per-topic study entry point.

Curriculum Download Flow manages the user experience for downloading curriculum content for offline use, including progress indication and error recovery during the download process. It has no detected inbound or outbound navigation edges, suggesting it is presented programmatically via a conditional state binding rather than through a named NavigationLink. It lives within CurriculumView.swift alongside the other curriculum screens, sharing the file's data model and view components. Without this screen, users would have no guided path to acquire offline curriculum content.

The Curriculum Help screen provides contextual documentation explaining how study curricula are structured and managed within UnaMentis. It is navigated to from the main Help screen and serves as a documentation leaf for users who need guidance on topic selection and progression logic. The content guides users through how to customize their learning path and interpret curriculum structure. It has no outbound navigation.

Curriculum is the entry-level list screen for browsing available curricula within the app. It has no inbound navigation edges from detected flows, indicating it is likely reached via a tab or a top-level menu entry that sits outside the detected navigation graph. It navigates forward to Curriculum Detail via a sheet, allowing users to select and inspect individual curricula before engaging with their topics. This screen is the user's starting point for the entire structured learning path and owns the initial curriculum selection interaction.

The Debug Conversation Test screen is a developer-facing tool for exercising the conversation pipeline outside of a live session. It is navigated to from the Settings hub and allows injection of test utterances and inspection of model responses, latency, and token usage. At 390 lines it provides a reasonably complete harness for testing dialogue turns end-to-end. It has no outbound navigation and is intended for development and support use.

The Device Metrics screen surfaces real-time hardware and runtime statistics such as CPU load, memory pressure, battery state, and thermal condition. It is navigated to from Settings and targets developers and power users diagnosing performance issues during extended sessions. At 326 lines it covers the key system metrics without being overly large. It has no outbound navigation and lives in the debug UI group.

The Diagnostics screen aggregates system health checks and log summaries to help developers and support staff identify configuration or runtime problems. It is reached from Settings and presents a structured view of recent errors, connectivity checks, and service reachability results. It shares the large SettingsView.swift file with several other settings-subtree screens. It has no outbound navigation.

Drill Session is the active SAT practice screen that the learner enters from the SAT Dashboard. It presents timed question-and-answer drills covering SAT subject domains and captures the learner's responses. The screen is implemented in a dedicated 244-line SwiftUI file. As a leaf screen with one inbound navigation edge and no outbound edges, it is the terminal destination of the SAT prep flow.

The Example Echo Dashboard is a template screen that demonstrates how a learning module's dashboard view should be structured within UnaMentis. It lives in the Template module alongside the Example Echo Root view and serves as a reference implementation for developers building new learning modules. As a template, it has no inbound navigation edges from production flows, making it an authoring guide rather than a user-facing feature. Developers can copy and adapt this pattern to scaffold a new module's top-level dashboard quickly.

The Example Echo Root is the entry-point view for the template echo module, demonstrating how a module's root navigation container should be structured. It shares the same source file as the Example Echo Dashboard (ExampleEchoModule.swift), indicating the two form a paired template: a root navigation shell plus an inner dashboard. It has no inbound edges from production navigation, so it exists solely as an authoring reference. Module developers copy and adapt this pattern when creating new UnaMentis learning modules.

The Freeform Chat Help screen explains the free-conversation mode in which users hold an open-ended voice dialogue with the AI tutor rather than following a structured question set. It is navigated to from the Help hub and acts as a documentation leaf. The content helps users understand when and how to use this mode effectively alongside structured study. It has no outbound navigation.

The Hands-Free Help screen documents the hands-free voice interaction mode, which lets users operate the app entirely through speech without touching the screen. It is navigated to from the Help hub and provides guidance on activating, using, and exiting this mode safely. The content covers wake word behavior and available voice commands during hands-free operation. It has no outbound navigation and is a documentation leaf.

The Help screen is the top-level documentation hub within the Settings area, reached from the main Settings view. It presents a navigable list of help topics and routes outward to five specialized help screens covering curriculum, freeform chat, hands-free mode, settings, and voice commands. Its role as a hub with five outbound edges makes it the single entry point into all contextual help content. Without it, none of the help topic screens are reachable through the normal navigation graph.

KBConference Training is a specialized Knowledge Bowl practice mode that simulates the pressure and format of a competitive conference-level Knowledge Bowl round. It is navigated to from KBDashboard via a push navigation transition and has no outbound navigation, delivering a self-contained training experience as a leaf screen. All scoring, round management, and question sequencing logic for this mode is contained within a single 857-line file. Its specialization in conference format distinguishes it from the more general domain drill and match simulation modes.

KBCreate Pack allows users to author or configure a custom Knowledge Bowl question pack for use in training sessions. It has no detected inbound or outbound navigation edges, suggesting it is reached via a programmatic trigger or a navigation path not captured by the static flow analyzer. As a leaf screen, it focuses entirely on question pack creation and does not launch further sub-flows. The packs created here would feed into the various Knowledge Bowl training modes as user-generated content.

KBDashboard is the central hub for the Knowledge Bowl feature set, providing navigation entry points to all major training modes and configuration screens. It has 8 outbound edges reaching every major Knowledge Bowl screen, making it the sole navigation controller for the entire KB section of the app. Users land here first when entering the Knowledge Bowl section and choose among oral sessions, written sessions, domain drills, rebound training, match simulation, conference training, quickstart settings, and KB settings. Without this screen, none of the Knowledge Bowl training modes would be reachable through the normal navigation flow.

KBDomain Drill is a targeted practice mode where users answer questions scoped to a specific Knowledge Bowl domain, building focused competency in one area at a time. It is reached via NavigationLink push from the KBDashboard and has no outbound navigation, encapsulating the entire domain drill session experience as a leaf screen. At 922 lines it carries significant complexity consistent with other heavy session views that manage real-time interaction state. Domain-specific performance data captured here contributes to overall mastery tracking.

KBDomain Mastery presents a progress overview for a specific Knowledge Bowl domain, showing mastery level, question coverage, and historical performance trends. It has no detected inbound or outbound navigation edges, suggesting it is presented programmatically from a context not captured by the static flow analyzer. As a read-only analytics view, it summarizes domain-level achievement without launching further sub-flows. Reviewers should confirm whether this screen is reachable via the dashboard or through a separate analytics path.

KBDomain Mix lets users configure a mixed-domain Knowledge Bowl session that draws questions from multiple domains simultaneously. It is presented as a sheet from the KBQuickstart Settings screen, making it part of the quick-start configuration flow rather than a standalone training mode entry. As a leaf screen with no outbound navigation, it focuses on domain selection before returning the result to the quickstart settings that invoked it. Its placement behind quickstart settings supports on-the-fly session customization without navigating away from the configuration modal.

KBEnhanced Validation Setup configures the AI-powered answer validation feature for Knowledge Bowl sessions, letting users tune how strictly spoken or written answers are evaluated by the LLM. It has no detected inbound or outbound navigation edges, placing it outside the statically detected navigation graph. This screen corresponds to the llmValidation feature flag seen in the app-level policy rules, and its configuration directly affects scoring fidelity for oral and written sessions. It is a supporting configuration screen that enables a premium capability.

The KB Getting Started Help screen provides introductory guidance for the Knowledge Bowl feature, explaining the game format, scoring rules, and how to begin a practice session. It lives in KBHelpSheet.swift alongside three other Knowledge Bowl help topics. It has no recorded inbound or outbound edges in the main navigation graph, suggesting it is presented contextually as a sheet from within the Knowledge Bowl game UI via paths not captured by the flow detector. It is a documentation leaf.

KBMatch Simulation replicates a competitive Knowledge Bowl match format with timed rounds and opponent simulation, giving users realistic tournament practice. It is navigated to from KBDashboard via NavigationLink and has no outbound navigation, hosting the entire match simulation experience in a single 943-line leaf screen. Match results and timing statistics from this screen contribute to overall performance tracking. It is one of the most feature-rich training modes given the complexity required to simulate a live opponent.

KBOral Session is the core spoken-answer practice mode where users answer Knowledge Bowl questions out loud and receive AI-driven speech recognition and validation feedback. It integrates with the STT and LLM pipeline reflected in the app-level event policy, handling stt_error, llm_error, and barge_in events during active sessions. It is navigated to from KBDashboard via NavigationLink and operates as a self-contained leaf screen. At 1,388 lines it is the second largest Knowledge Bowl screen, reflecting the complexity of managing real-time audio capture, transcription, and AI scoring within a single view.

KBQuickstart Settings is a configuration sheet that lets users rapidly customize a Knowledge Bowl session before launching it, including domain mix selection and core session parameters. It is presented as a sheet from KBDashboard and itself opens the KBDomain Mix sheet for domain selection, making it a connector node that bridges the dashboard to the domain picker across two modal levels. Updated configuration flows back to the dashboard on dismissal to initialize the selected session mode. Its position in the flow means errors or state loss here prevent the user from reaching any training session via the quickstart path.

KBRebound Training focuses on questions the user previously answered incorrectly, creating a targeted review loop that converts missed questions into mastered material. It is navigated to from KBDashboard via NavigationLink and has no further outbound navigation, making it a leaf session screen. At 1,134 lines it carries moderate complexity, likely managing a dynamically constructed retry queue alongside real-time scoring and correction tracking. This mode is important for users who want to close specific knowledge gaps identified in earlier sessions.

The KB Regional Rules Help screen explains the regional tournament rule variations that affect Knowledge Bowl scoring and question eligibility. It shares KBHelpSheet.swift with three sibling Knowledge Bowl help screens. It has no recorded inbound or outbound edges, indicating it is likely presented as a sheet from within the Knowledge Bowl game screens via paths not captured in the flow graph. It is a documentation leaf.

KBSettings provides Knowledge Bowl-specific configuration options such as default session lengths, scoring strictness, and preferences scoped to the Knowledge Bowl feature area. It is presented as a sheet from KBDashboard and is co-located in the same source file (KBDashboardView.swift), indicating tight coupling with the dashboard's state. As a leaf settings sheet with no outbound navigation, it handles all in-KB preferences without navigating away from the Knowledge Bowl section. Updated preferences flow back to the dashboard when the sheet is dismissed.

The KB Strategy Help screen offers tips and tactics for competing effectively in Knowledge Bowl matches, covering buzzer timing, team coordination, and subject prioritization. It is co-located with three other Knowledge Bowl help topics in KBHelpSheet.swift. It has no recorded inbound or outbound navigation edges, suggesting it is surfaced contextually from the game flow rather than the main Settings navigation tree. It is a documentation leaf.

The KB Training Modes Help screen describes the different practice modes available in the Knowledge Bowl feature, such as timed drills, category focus, and team versus solo play. It is co-located in KBHelpSheet.swift alongside three other Knowledge Bowl help screens. Like its siblings, it has no recorded inbound or outbound edges in the main navigation graph and is likely presented as a contextual sheet from within the Knowledge Bowl UI. It is a documentation leaf.

KBWritten Session is the text-entry answer practice mode for Knowledge Bowl, where users type their answers rather than speaking them. It is navigated to from KBDashboard via NavigationLink and provides a self-contained written quiz experience in a single 553-line leaf screen. Unlike the oral session, it does not require the STT pipeline, making it available when microphone access is unavailable or when users prefer a silent practice environment. It complements KBOralSession by offering an alternative input modality for the same question content.

Kyutai Pocket Settings configures the on-device Kyutai speech model used for speech-to-text within the app, providing controls for model selection, microphone sensitivity, and audio capture parameters. It has no inbound navigation edges in the detected flow graph, suggesting it is reached via the More tab or a settings hierarchy not captured statically. From here, users can open an audio recorder sheet to test and calibrate their microphone input before committing to a configuration. This screen is key for users tuning the STT pipeline that underpins oral Knowledge Bowl sessions and any other voice-input features.

Modules presents a browsable list of learning modules available to the user, organized as discrete units of study content that sit alongside but separate from the structured curriculum flow. It has no detected inbound or outbound navigation edges, suggesting it is reachable via the Learning tab or a programmatic trigger not captured in the flow graph. As an isolated list screen it likely serves as an alternate entry point into learning content alongside the Curriculum path. Reviewers should determine whether this screen is an independent content catalog or a gateway to the same sessions reached through the Curriculum hierarchy.

The Onboarding Consent Page presents the privacy policy and data usage consent form that new users must review and accept before using UnaMentis. At 124 lines it is a focused, single-purpose screen. It has no recorded inbound or outbound navigation edges, indicating it is presented inline within the onboarding sequence as an embedded TabView page rather than a standalone push destination. It is a compliance gate in the first-run experience.

The Onboarding Page is a reusable page template used to render individual feature-introduction slides within the onboarding carousel, displaying illustrations and explanatory text for each slide. It lives in OnboardingView.swift alongside the Onboarding container view. It has no recorded inbound or outbound edges because it is composed directly by the parent Onboarding view as an embedded page rather than pushed via navigation. It is a structural building block of the first-run experience.

The Onboarding view presents the first-run experience for new users, guiding them through the app's key features before they reach the main interface. It is presented as a fullscreen cover from Settings, allowing existing users who want to review the onboarding flow to re-enter it on demand. At 292 lines it manages the page carousel, progress indicators, and completion handling. It has no outbound navigation after the user completes or dismisses the flow.

The On-Device LLM Settings screen configures the locally running language model used for on-device inference, covering model selection, memory allocation limits, and inference quality trade-offs. It is navigated to from Settings and is relevant when users opt for a privacy-preserving local inference backend instead of a cloud API. At 502 lines it handles the nuanced configuration surface for on-device model management. It has no outbound navigation.

Oral Exam Dashboard is an iOS SwiftUI screen that serves as the entry point to the Oral Exam module, presenting the user with past session history, configuration options, and a start action. It navigates to Oral Exam Session when the user initiates a new exam, making it the sole gateway into the oral exam interactive flow. Both this view and its destination share the 655-line OralExamViews.swift file. A reviewer arriving at this screen sees everything needed to understand a user's oral exam history and launch a new session.

The Oral Exam Feedback view presents the post-examination evaluation to the user after an oral exam session concludes. It is sourced from OralExamViews.swift, which at 655 lines also contains the live session UI, indicating it is rendered as a distinct phase within the oral exam flow rather than a separate navigation destination. The view displays AI-generated feedback covering the student's preparation, presentation, and questioning stages. It is the final screen users see in the oral exam module before returning to the main navigation.

Oral Exam Session is the active examination screen where the user speaks answers to questions and receives AI-graded feedback. It is navigated to exclusively from Oral Exam Dashboard and has no outbound navigation, functioning as a terminal interactive session view. Sharing the 655-line OralExamViews.swift file with the dashboard, it contains the bulk of the oral exam interaction logic including microphone management, response display, and scoring presentation. It is the primary value-delivery screen of the Oral Exam module.

The Provider Test screen allows developers and advanced users to send a test prompt to the currently configured AI provider and inspect the raw response, latency, and token usage. It is accessed from Settings and lives in the large SettingsView.swift file alongside other settings subtree screens. Its purpose is to validate provider configuration before committing to a full session. It has no outbound navigation and is a diagnostic leaf.

The QBDashboard view is the entry screen for the Quiz Bowl module, giving users an overview of their practice history and a launch point for new sessions. At 131 lines it is a focused summary screen that surfaces aggregated performance data so users can decide what to practice next. It links to the practice session and metrics panel views that together form the Quiz Bowl experience. As a leaf UI screen with no detected outbound navigation, it acts as a standalone overview within the module.

The QBMetrics Panel is a small, focused SwiftUI view (72 lines) that renders performance metrics for the Quiz Bowl module, intended to be embedded within the QBDashboard or practice session view as a reusable component. It displays quantitative information such as correct answer rates, streaks, and session counts. Being only 72 lines, it is a pure display component with no business logic of its own. Its role is to provide a concise visual summary of a learner's Quiz Bowl progress wherever that summary is needed.

The QBPractice Session view is the live interactive screen for a Quiz Bowl practice session, spanning 308 lines to accommodate question presentation, voice answer capture, evaluation feedback, timer display, and streak tracking. It drives the user through the round lifecycle from item presentation through answer evaluation. The view coordinates with the Knowledge Bowl module to handle voice answer capture and AI-based evaluation, and it responds reactively to events such as round start, answer window open, evaluation results, and round end. Users spend the majority of their Quiz Bowl time on this screen.

The QR Code Scanner screen opens the device camera to scan a QR code encoding server connection details, eliminating manual URL and credential entry. It is presented as a sheet from the Server Settings screen and passes scanned connection parameters back to that screen on dismissal. At 354 lines it handles camera permission requests, live preview rendering, and barcode decoding. It has no further outbound navigation.

The Quick Stats view displays a compact summary of the user's recent session performance, such as accuracy rate and session count, designed for at-a-glance review without navigating into the full analytics breakdown. It is co-located with the full Analytics screen in AnalyticsView.swift and is likely embedded as a composable sub-view within that screen. It has no recorded inbound or outbound navigation edges. It surfaces the most actionable metrics efficiently.

Reading List is a SwiftUI screen that presents the user's collection of saved reading items such as articles, documents, or links queued for later consumption. At 307 lines it carries meaningful display and interaction logic for browsing and managing the reading queue. No inbound navigation edges are recorded, suggesting it is a top-level tab destination. It is the entry point to the reading workflow, leading users toward the Reader and Playback screens.

Reading Playback is a SwiftUI screen that provides audio or text-to-speech playback controls for a reading item, letting users listen to content rather than read it. At 232 lines it contains transport controls, playback progress, and likely speed or voice configuration. No navigation edges are recorded in either direction, suggesting it is presented modally or as a subview from Reading List or Reading Reader. It extends the reading experience to audio-first or multitasking scenarios.

Reading Reader is a SwiftUI screen that renders the full text of a reading item for in-app consumption. At 398 lines it is the largest reading-related screen, suggesting rich features such as font controls, scroll tracking, highlight support, or progress persistence. The Audio module is the foundational voice pipeline for UnaMentis, managing the AVAudioEngine lifecycle, audio session configuration, TTS output, live speech capture, segment caching, pre-generation invalidation, and barge-in detection. The Config module manages all runtime configuration for UnaMentis, including API key storage and retrieval, LLM provider metadata, remote model definitions, and server endpoint discovery. It embeds cost estimation calculations for each supported provider across STT, TTS, and LLM usage, enabling the routing layer to make cost-aware decisions at runtime. The ServerConfigManager handles both static configuration and live endpoint discovery with health status tracking. Every module that calls an external AI service depends on this module to resolve the correct endpoint, credentials, and cost parameters.

The Context module manages what information is included in each LLM prompt turn, assembling field-of-view (FOV) excerpts from the document the user is reading, conversation buffer history, confidence scores, and on-demand topic summaries. The FOVContextManager and ReadingFOVContextManager track which part of the curriculum the user is focused on and inject the surrounding content into prompts to keep AI responses grounded. The ContextSummarizer caches results to avoid redundant LLM calls when the same topic content is summarized multiple times. Without this module, the AI tutor would respond without awareness of the material being studied.

The Curriculum module is the core learning content engine, responsible for loading, parsing, and managing curricula in the UnaMentis Curriculum Format (UMCF). It tracks per-topic progress including time spent, quiz scores, teachback attempts, and mastery levels, and computes aggregate metrics such as completion percentage and average quiz score across a curriculum. The DocumentProcessor ingests source files into the curriculum model, and the SampleCurriculumSeeder populates the app with demonstration content. This module is the source of truth for what a user is learning and how far they have progressed.

The Discovery module implements a multi-tier server discovery system that locates the UnaMentis backend inference server on the local network before any AI-driven session can begin. It orchestrates six strategies in priority order: cached results, Bonjour mDNS, MultipeerConnectivity, subnet scan, manual entry, and QR code, reporting fractional progress across tiers as it proceeds. It maps failures to typed error cases covering timeout, network unavailability, invalid response, health-check failure, cancellation, and tier-not-available. Without successful server discovery the app cannot reach the AI inference endpoint, making this module a critical prerequisite for all voice and exam functionality.

The Tiers module contains the concrete implementations of three automatic discovery strategies invoked by the parent Discovery orchestrator: BonjourDiscovery browses for mDNS services, CachedServerDiscovery reads previously resolved addresses from persistent storage, and SubnetScanDiscovery probes addresses across the local subnet. Each tier handles NWConnection state transitions (ready, failed, cancelled) and resolves NWEndpoint host variants including IPv4 addresses, IPv6 addresses, and DNS hostnames. Failure across all three automatic tiers forces the user to fall back to manual entry or QR code scan.

The KnowledgeBowl core module is the domain engine for the Knowledge Bowl study feature, containing all data models, session management, and business logic for quiz-based learning. It manages KBPacks (content bundles), KBQuestions, KBSessions with timed countdowns, KBDomainMix for weighted domain distribution, KBRegionalConfig for region-specific content rules, and KBLocalPackStore for offline pack persistence. Twelve calculation rules govern weight normalization, time-remaining computation, accuracy scoring, and per-domain statistics. It is the shared engine consumed by both the iOS and watchOS UI layers for all Knowledge Bowl functionality.

The Team module extends the KnowledgeBowl core with multi-member team support, storing per-member statistics and managing domain assignments across a roster. It contains KBTeamMember, KBTeamProfile, KBMemberStats, and KBDomainAssignment, with twelve calculation rules covering rolling accuracy updates, weighted average response time, coverage percentage, and aggregate team performance. Domain assignments are typed as primary, secondary, or suggested, enabling differentiated roles within a competing team. This module enables Knowledge Bowl practice in a team competition context where individual contributions aggregate to a shared team profile.

The Modules component is the foundational plugin architecture for UnaMentis, defining the contracts and registry that all learning engine modules must implement. It provides the ModuleProtocol that every engine (Drill, OralExam, QuizMatch) conforms to, along with ModuleRegistry for discovery, ModuleHost for lifecycle management, and ModuleService for runtime coordination. ModuleCatalog and ModuleManifest handle module metadata and configuration, while ConformanceDrivable provides a protocol for conformance-based module driving. Error handling covers the full spectrum from network failures to decoding errors, suggesting modules are fetched and loaded dynamically at runtime.

The Drill engine implements a spaced-repetition or flashcard-style learning mode within the UnaMentis module system. DrillEngine contains the runtime logic for running a drill session, DrillFormatDescriptor describes how the drill format is configured and presented to the module host, and DrillModels holds the data structures for drill content and session state. The engine enforces a two-tier policy distinguishing free versus review items, which likely gates content access by subscription or learning progress. At 802 lines across three files, it is a focused, self-contained engine implementation.

The OralExam engine is the most complex learning engine in UnaMentis, implementing a spoken-language examination system with multi-stage simulation (preparation, presentation, questioning) and multi-dimensional scoring across delivery, clarity, structure, argumentation, and interaction. ExaminerBrain drives the AI-powered examiner logic, OralExamEngine manages the real-time session clock (with nanosecond-precision tick scheduling), OralExamDeliveryMetrics tracks speaking time and trailing silence, and OralExamModels and OralExamFormatDescriptor define the data contracts. Scoring uses a rubric averaging formula over named dimensions, and delivery metrics strip trailing silence from speaking duration to produce accurate engagement measurements.

The QuizMatch engine implements a competitive quiz format where participants buzz in to answer questions, supporting both team and individual scoring modes. QuizMatchEngine manages session flow and scoring, QuizMatchFormatDescriptor provides the configuration contract for the module host, and QuizMatchModels defines participant, score, and match state structures. The participant index calculation clamps inputs to valid bounds, preventing out-of-range crashes when buzz events arrive. At 1155 lines it sits between the Drill and OralExam engines in complexity.

The Services module is the heavyweight cross-cutting service layer that all engines depend on for evaluation, content, progress tracking, and telemetry. ContentStoreService manages learning content retrieval, ProgressStoreService persists learner progress, ModuleTelemetryService records usage events, LLMRubricEvaluator submits answer exchanges to a language model for rubric-based scoring, and DefaultResponseEvaluationService plus EvaluationMatchers/Normalization/Synonyms implement a local n-gram and fuzzy-match evaluation pipeline. The evaluation pipeline uses a weighted combination of unigram, bigram, and trigram scores alongside Levenshtein distance, with synonym expansion and fuzzy thresholds tuned per candidate. The LLM evaluator constructs structured conversation transcripts from exchange pairs and forwards them to an external model, meaning this component creates a critical runtime dependency on an external AI service.

ManagedObjects contains the Core Data entity classes that persist all user data across app launches, including curricula, documents, reading list items, reading chunks with duration estimates, bookmarks, visual assets, reinforcement review items, and session records. It computes derived values such as reading progress percentage and remaining reading time directly on managed object instances using stored chunk word counts. This layer is the durable store for everything a user has imported, read, or learned. Any data loss or schema corruption here would be catastrophic to the user experience.

The Questions module defines the canonical representation of a learning question and provides utilities for transforming and cleaning question text before it is presented to users or sent to the LLM. CanonicalQuestion standardizes question objects across the app's multiple quiz and exam formats. QuestionTransformer adapts canonical questions to the requirements of specific drill or exam contexts. TextCleaner normalizes raw text from content packs, removing formatting artifacts that would degrade voice playback or display quality.

The ReadingList module manages the user's collection of reading materials, supporting PDF, plain text, Markdown, and web article sources through a unified manager. It fetches web articles via WebArticleFetcher, extracts readable text from HTML via HTMLArticleExtractor, strips Markdown formatting for voice playback, and chunks long texts into timed reading segments with estimated durations. The ReadingListManager coordinates item lifecycle from unread through in-progress to completed or archived. This module feeds the FOV context system with the material the user is actively reading.

The Routing Models module defines the data types that govern how the app selects which LLM endpoint handles each request, including endpoint definitions, task type classifications, routing conditions, and the routing table itself. It models multi-provider support for OpenAI, Anthropic, self-hosted, and on-device models across a rich taxonomy of task types such as tutoring response, Socratic question, document summarization, and transcript generation. Routing conditions evaluate device state (thermal, memory, battery, network latency) and endpoint health to select the optimal backend at runtime. Per-token cost calculations are embedded in the endpoint model to enable cost-aware routing decisions.

The Session module is the conversational heart of the UnaMentis iOS app, containing SessionManager, MetricsUploadService, MetricsUploadQueue, and ResponsePreGenerator. SessionManager drives a full state machine across states including idle, aiSpeaking, userSpeaking, aiThinking, processingUserUtterance, paused, interrupted, and error, coordinating the round-trip between speech recognition, LLM inference, and text-to-speech. MetricsUploadService computes per-turn costs in three dimensions: LLM token cost (Decimal per input and output token), TTS character cost (Decimal per character), and STT duration cost (Decimal per hour), then queues these for upload to the telemetry endpoint. ResponsePreGenerator anticipates upcoming AI turns to pre-warm responses and reduce perceived latency. Without this module the app has no session lifecycle, no cost accounting, and no ability to manage multi-turn AI conversations.

The Telemetry module instruments the end-to-end voice pipeline latency for UnaMentis, measuring time-to-first-audio (TTFA), STT emission delay, LLM first-token latency, and TTS time-to-first-byte. It records quality events including thermal state changes, context compression, user interruptions, and adaptive quality adjustments across sessions. The MetricsExporter serializes and sends measurements to an external endpoint, while TTFAInstrumentation focuses on the specific latency from when the user stops speaking to when the AI first produces sound. This module is the primary tool for diagnosing performance regressions in the voice pipeline.

The Todo module tracks the user's active learning task queue, managing items that originate from manual user action, voice commands, auto-resume logic, or reinforcement scheduling. The CurriculumSuggestionService recommends next steps based on the current state of the curriculum. TodoManager persists items through a pending, in-progress, completed, and archived lifecycle, connecting the curriculum engine's content to the user's immediate learning agenda.

The Tools module implements the LLM function-calling interface, enabling the AI tutor to take structured actions during a conversation such as adding todo items or marking topics for review. TodoToolHandler and WebSearchToolHandler are the two concrete action handlers, bridging the AI's intent to act with the app's data layer.

The Intents module exposes UnaMentis functionality to Siri and the Shortcuts app through the App Intents framework, enabling users to resume learning, start a lesson, show progress, or begin a conversation without opening the app. It defines CurriculumEntity and TopicEntity as queryable App Intent entities backed by Core Data, and the AppShortcutsProvider registers phrase triggers for voice activation. The AuralSkills module is a self-contained ear training feature that drills users on musical intervals, chords, tonality, cadences, and solfege. The module handles voice command parsing (quit, skip, repeatLast) and maps synonym phrases to canonical music theory terms before sending answers for evaluation. It integrates with the Audio module for playback and the LLM for answer judgment.

The KnowledgeBowl module implements competitive Knowledge Bowl and Quiz Bowl practice, where questions are read aloud and users buzz in to answer before the question finishes. The module manages the full match lifecycle through match start, conference start, answer window, evaluation, skip, and match end events. Voice commands (quit, skip) allow hands-free session control.

The OralExam module simulates formal oral examination formats including the French Grand Oral, practice vivas, and free question volleys, loaded from JSON format descriptors. The session proceeds through preparation, presentation, and questioning stages with countdown timers, and the OralExamSessionViewModel manages state transitions through notStarted, runningStage, assemblingFeedback, feedback, and completed phases. Format-specific rules are loaded from descriptor files, allowing new exam formats to be added without code changes.

QuizBowl is the top-level module that ties together the quiz bowl feature, providing content loading, question mapping, statistics persistence, and module conformance wiring.
