The Models sub-module defines the core data structures for the quiz bowl feature: question formats (QBFormat), individual quiz items (QBItem), and performance metrics (QBMetrics). It is a pure data layer with two inbound edges, meaning both the ML sub-module and the LLM service depend on these types to describe questions and evaluate answers. Having no outbound edges confirms it is a foundational leaf in the dependency graph that other modules build on top of. Keeping formats, items, and metrics separated into three files allows each concern to evolve independently without coupling.

The Views sub-module renders all quiz bowl user-facing screens, including a dashboard, a metrics panel, and a full practice session view backed by a dedicated view model. The practice session drives a complex state machine through six states (not started, reading question, awaiting answer, bonus, showing feedback, completed) and handles a rich event stream covering speech narration, listening, answer capture, and evaluation. Reading duration is computed dynamically from word count and a words-per-second constant, and a reading fraction is clamped to 1.0 to drive progress affordances. With 1,036 lines across four files and no test coverage, it is the largest and most behaviourally complex untested surface in the quiz bowl feature.

The SATPrep module delivers vocabulary and math drill sessions designed for SAT preparation, presenting items from bundled content packs and evaluating voice answers using the LLM. The DrillSessionModel drives each session through idle, loading, presenting, awaiting answer, feedback, and completed phases, tracking streaks and per-item correctness. The SATDashboardView gives users a progress overview before starting a session. Content integrity is validated against pack manifests to detect missing or corrupted items before a session begins.

The AuralSkills resource pack provides the bundled JSON content that seeds the ear training module with its initial drill items at first launch. It consists of a manifest file declaring the pack's metadata and integrity information, and an items file containing structured musical drill entries covering intervals, chords, tonality, cadences, and solfege. The AuralSkills module validates the manifest before loading items to detect corruption or version mismatches. Without this pack, the AuralSkills module would have no content to present and would fail to start a drill session.

The ContentPacks directory bundles the initial set of practice content that ships with the app, covering IHBB Europe trivia, NAQT Quiz Bowl questions, SAT math mental drills, and SAT vocabulary in context across 10 files. Each format consists of a paired manifest and items file; manifests declare integrity checksums and metadata while items files contain the actual question content. These packs are the primary content source for the Knowledge Bowl, Quiz Bowl, and SAT Prep modules on first launch. Additional content packs can be added here to extend the app's subject coverage.

FormatDescriptors holds the JSON configuration files that define the rules and structure for each supported exam and competition format, including French Grand Oral (full and practice), IHBB Europe, Colorado Knowledge Bowl, practice viva, ACF Quiz Bowl, and NAQT skeleton and full formats. The OralExam and KnowledgeBowl modules read these descriptors at session start to configure timing, stage sequences, question handling, and scoring behavior. Adding a new competition format requires only a new JSON file here rather than any Swift code changes. These descriptors are the source of truth for all format-specific behavior in the app.

The OralSyllabus resource pack provides the bundled starter topics that seed the Oral Exam module's topic selection for viva-style practice sessions. It consists of a manifest declaring pack integrity metadata and an items file containing topic definitions with associated subject areas and difficulty levels. The OralExam module reads these items when the user selects a topic for a practice viva session. Without this pack, topic-driven oral exam sessions would have no pre-loaded subject matter to draw from and the topic selection step would fail.

The Curriculum service layer is responsible for fetching, caching, and streaming educational content from the UnaMentis backend. It contains four collaborating files: CurriculumDownloadManager handles asset retrieval and tracks download progress (with a weighted formula: 70% base plus 25% scaled by cached-to-total asset ratio), CurriculumService manages topic metadata and decoding, TranscriptStreamingService streams transcript content and coordinates TTS voice selection (VibeVoice or Piper), and VisualAssetCache persists downloaded visual media. This module is the primary conduit between the network backend and the session UI. The breadth of error cases it handles, spanning network failures, server errors, decoding issues, and TTS server exhaustion, reflects its role as the core content pipeline.

FeatureFlags provides remote-controlled configuration for the app, allowing string, number, and JSON-typed flags to be fetched, cached, and evaluated at runtime without an app release. The module tracks a cache hit rate (cacheHits / totalEvaluations) to monitor efficiency, and enforces authentication by handling 401 and 403 HTTP responses. It is structured into four files: FeatureFlagKeys enumerates known flag names, FeatureFlagTypes defines the value union and error types, FeatureFlagCache manages persistence, and FeatureFlagService owns the fetch-and-evaluate lifecycle. With no edges in the current graph, it is consumed by other modules via direct import rather than through a tracked dependency.

KnowledgeBowl is the primary service layer for all quiz bowl game mechanics, covering match orchestration, question delivery, pack management, analytics, conference timing, evaluation bridging, and progress tracking. It exposes adapters that connect the quiz bowl UI module to the underlying match engine and progress systems, acting as the domain logic hub for competitive academic quiz bowl. Accuracy and domain strength calculations are performed across session aggregates, and conference time pressure is factored into scoring via a normalized time-limit ratio. With twelve files and 3,833 lines, it is the heaviest single service in the feature and the runtime backbone that all quiz bowl interactions depend on.

The ML sub-module provides on-device and remote machine learning capabilities for the quiz bowl feature, specifically sentence embeddings and LLM-based answer validation. KBEmbeddingsService downloads a CoreML sentence-embeddings package from models.unamentis.com and uses it to compute semantic similarity between student answers and expected answers. KBLLMValidator applies a language model to judge answer correctness when embedding similarity alone is insufficient. It has two outbound edges: one to the quiz bowl models (to understand question and answer types) and one to the root unamentis domain (fetching the ML model package). Error handling covers the full lifecycle from download failure through dimension mismatch during inference.

The Team sub-module manages team roster data and synchronization for quiz bowl competitions, supporting server, local, and offline sync modes. KBTeamStore holds team membership state, KBLocalTeamSync handles local-first persistence and import, and KBTeamSyncProtocol defines the interface that allows the sync strategy to be swapped at runtime. Error cases cover missing team profiles, member-not-found by ID, sync failures, and import failures, giving the module a well-defined failure surface across all three sync modes. With no inbound or outbound edges recorded, it operates as a self-contained service consumed by other parts of the application through the sync protocol abstraction.

The LLM service module is the multi-provider AI inference layer for the application, supporting Anthropic, Google AI, OpenAI, on-device models (Gemma, Qwen, Ministral), self-hosted endpoints, and a mock implementation for development. It abstracts provider differences behind a common interface, selects on-device models based on available physical RAM (6 GB, 8 GB, and 12 GB tiers), tracks token usage costs, and manages the full on-device model lifecycle from download through loading and inference. It has one outbound edge to the quiz bowl models, indicating it delivers evaluated or generated content back into the quiz bowl domain. The fallback service ensures graceful degradation when a preferred provider is unavailable.

Protocols defines the Swift protocol interfaces that abstract the four core AI service categories in UnaMentis: LLM (language model inference), STT (speech-to-text), TTS (text-to-speech), and VAD (voice activity detection). Each protocol file enumerates the concrete provider options the app supports, for example STT covers AssemblyAI, Deepgram Nova 3, OpenAI Whisper, Groq Whisper, Apple Speech, GLM ASR, and Parakeet EOU. By programming to these protocols rather than concrete implementations, the rest of the app can swap providers at runtime without changing calling code. This module is the architectural seam that makes the multi-provider AI pipeline composable.

ReadingPlayback manages the audio playback pipeline for the Reading List feature, including pre-generation of TTS audio for articles and chunk-based sequential playback. ReadingAudioPreGenerator synthesizes speech for article segments ahead of consumption, ReadingPlaybackService coordinates playback state and buffer management, and ReadingTTSCache stores pre-generated audio at 24000 Hz (matching PocketTTS and platform TTS output rates). The module handles error states including buffer timeouts and invalid chunk indices. It is consumed by the ReadingList UI module to provide smooth, low-latency article audio.

The STT module implements speech-to-text transcription across seven concrete providers: Apple Speech (on-device), AssemblyAI, Deepgram, Fluid Audio, GLM ASR (both server and on-device variants), Groq Whisper, and a health monitor for GLM ASR availability. Each provider adapts to the STT protocol defined in the Protocols module, handling audio format conversion (WAV header construction at byteRate = sampleRate x blockAlign), WebSocket streaming for real-time providers, and HTTP POST for batch providers. The Groq provider calls the external Groq API for transcription. At 3631 lines across 11 files, this is one of the larger service modules and sits on the critical path for all voice-driven interactions.

The TTS module implements text-to-speech synthesis across nine concrete providers: Apple TTS (on-device AVSpeechSynthesizer), Chatterbox, Deepgram Aura 2, ElevenLabs Flash and Turbo, Kyutai PocketTTS (on-device neural), PlayHT, VibeVoice, and a self-hosted option. It is the largest service module at 4986 lines across 11 files, reflecting the complexity of supporting both streaming cloud providers and on-device neural models. Voice character selection is supported with eight named voices (alba, marius, javert, jean, fantine, cosette, eponine, azelma) and 23 language options. The Kyutai PocketTTS path includes a model manager for on-device ML lifecycle. Deepgram is an external service dependency on the critical audio output path.

VAD (Voice Activity Detection) implements two concrete detection backends: Silero VAD (a neural on-device model) and Fluid Audio VAD. Both implementations handle audio buffer resampling to match the required input sample rate (ratio = targetSampleRate / buffer.format.sampleRate), ensuring the detector receives audio in the expected format regardless of the device capture rate. VAD is the gating component that determines when the user is speaking versus silent, directly controlling when the STT pipeline activates. Without accurate VAD, the conversation loop either misses utterances or floods STT with silence.

The Voice module provides the ambient voice UX layer that sits above raw STT: VoiceCommandRecognizer maps recognized speech to discrete commands (ready, submit, next, skip, repeatLast, quit, bookmark, flag), VoiceActivityFeedback plays tonal audio cues for each command outcome (commandRecognized, correct, incorrect, bookmarkSaved, etc.), VoiceBookmarkService persists bookmark events triggered by voice, and FlaggableActivity defines the protocol for content items that can be flagged hands-free. It uses UIKit (likely for AVAudioPlayer or AudioServicesPlaySystemSound) to deliver haptic-adjacent audio feedback. This module is what makes the app genuinely voice-driven rather than merely voice-aware.

WebSearch wraps the Brave Search API to provide web query capability to the app, likely used during curriculum content generation or fact enrichment. BraveSearchService implements the HTTP request lifecycle including API key injection, rate limit handling (HTTP 429), and quota exhaustion detection (HTTP 402). WebSearchProvider defines the protocol abstraction so alternative search backends could be swapped in. At 246 lines across two files, this is a focused, single-responsibility module. No graph edges indicate it is imported directly by consumers rather than referenced through a tracked dependency.

BargeInHarness is a specialized test infrastructure module for measuring barge-in detection quality: the ability of the app to detect and respond to a user speaking while the AI is talking. It provides a test corpus of audio clips categorized as command, engagement, noise, or echo, a measurement harness that plays clips and records detection outcomes, and a metrics collector that reports results per category and thermal state. The harness generates synthetic audio via TTS, plays back pre-recorded files, or injects noise, and accounts for device thermal throttling (nominal through critical) as a confounding variable. It is a developer-facing benchmarking tool with no production call path.

KBAudioTestHarness is the primary audio pipeline testing infrastructure for Knowledge Bowl and related features. It provides audio generation (tones, speech synthesis), audio injection into live pipelines, test case orchestration, result collection, and transcript validation using Levenshtein edit-distance (with a 25% threshold: max(2, 0.25 x expectedWordCount)). The harness supports four audio source types: generated TTS, pre-recorded files, bundled assets, and raw PCM data. At 2172 lines across 7 files including its own CLAUDE.md, it is a substantial testing system with explicit AI agent instructions. It operates entirely within the test target and has no production call path.

LatencyHarness is a performance benchmarking system that measures end-to-end voice pipeline latency across all STT provider configurations. It coordinates test runs (LatencyTestCoordinator), collects per-stage timing data (LatencyMetricsCollector), captures CPU usage (totalCPU = cpuUsage / TH_USAGE_SCALE x 100), and produces structured test results. It supports all eight STT providers (Deepgram Nova3, AssemblyAI, Apple Speech, GLM ASR Nano, GLM ASR OnDevice, Parakeet EOU, OpenAI Whisper, Groq Whisper). Progress is tracked as completedConfigurations / totalConfigurations x 100. At 3081 lines across 6 files including its own CLAUDE.md, it is the largest test infrastructure component.

Components is the shared UI component library for the UnaMentis app, containing reusable SwiftUI views used across feature modules. It includes BrandLogo for consistent brand identity, CoreDataErrorView for surfacing persistence errors, FormulaRendererView for rendering mathematical formulas and equations, HelpComponents providing contextual in-app help UI, and SessionControlComponents for session-level controls (play, pause, stop) in three size variants (compact, standard, large). At 1963 lines across 5 files, it is a substantial shared library consumed by feature modules without requiring them to implement common UI patterns.

The Curriculum UI module presents the browsable curriculum catalog and topic selection interface. CurriculumView renders the full curriculum with difficulty levels (beginner, intermediate, advanced) and download state (notStarted, inProgress, completed, reviewing), while TopicSelectionView allows the learner to pick specific topics. It includes an inline help sheet (CurriculumHelpSheet) built with the shared HelpComponents. At 1878 lines across 2 files, it is a content-dense view that coordinates with the Curriculum service module for download state and decoding errors. It is consumed by the Learning module which hosts the curriculum/modules navigation tab.

The Debug module provides developer-facing tools for testing and profiling the conversation pipeline from within the app. DebugConversationTestView and its view model allow developers to run scripted conversation tests (greeting, factualQA, conceptExplain) against all five LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, selfHosted, localMLX), viewing the full conversation history with role-colored entries (user, assistant, system, error). DeviceMetricsView surfaces real-time device health indicators (good, warning, critical, unknown) including thermal state. At 1185 lines across 3 files, it exposes full session state visibility including the eight-value session state machine (idle through processingUserUtterance).

KnowledgeBowl is the largest UI module at 10661 lines across 18 files, implementing the full Knowledge Bowl competition and practice feature set. It includes a dashboard, domain drill view, domain mastery view, domain mix view, conference training view, pack creation view, enhanced validation setup, and domain-specific charts and analytics. It tracks learner XP (totalXP / 100 + 1 = level, capped at 10), time per question, accuracy (correctCount / totalQuestions), and session duration. The Levenshtein edit distance calculation present here (for answer matching) mirrors the implementation in KBAudioTestHarness, suggesting shared answer-validation logic. This module is the primary competitive practice surface of the app.

Learning is the top-level UI container for the educational content area, hosting two sub-sections: Curriculum (browsable lessons and downloads) and Modules (structured learning units). LearningView manages the top-level section tab state (curriculum vs. modules) and delegates rendering to the appropriate sub-view, while ModulesView renders the structured module list. At 1166 lines across 2 files, it acts as a navigation hub between the curriculum catalog and the structured module pathway. With no inbound edges, it is reached from the main tab bar.

Onboarding presents the first-run experience for new users, consisting of an OnboardingView that walks through app introduction steps and a ConsentView that presents the privacy policy (hosted at unamentis.org/privacy.html) for user acceptance. Completion of onboarding transitions the user into the main app experience, which is modeled as an outbound HTTP edge to the unamentis root target. At 416 lines across 2 files, it is deliberately concise to minimize friction at first launch. The consent gate makes this a compliance-critical flow.

ReadingList is the UI module for the article reading and audio playback feature, allowing users to import articles via URL, read them in a reader view with inline images, and listen to AI-generated audio narration. It contains a full MVVM stack: ReadingListViewModel manages the article collection with active/completed/archived filtering, ReadingPlaybackViewModel coordinates chunk-based audio playback state (progress = currentChunkIndex / totalChunks), and three dedicated views cover the list, reader, and playback surfaces. URLImportSheet handles importing new articles by URL. Voice commands (bookmark, flag) are supported during playback.

Session is the primary interactive learning session UI, the core runtime experience of the app where AI-driven conversation, visual assets, and progress tracking converge. SessionView manages the full eight-state session machine (idle, userSpeaking, aiThinking, aiSpeaking, interrupted, paused, processingUserUtterance, error) and coordinates TTS provider selection across all eight supported providers. MapAssetView renders geographic map assets (standard, satellite, hybrid) and VisualAssetView handles equations and formula assets. Progress is computed as completedSegmentCount / totalSegments. At 5001 lines across 3 files, it is the most complex production UI module. Watch commands (pause, resume, mute, unmute, stop) flow through the session state machine.

The Settings module is the largest UI surface in the UnaMentis iOS app at 8816 lines across 15 files, covering API provider configuration, barge-in sensitivity tuning, Chatterbox and Kyutai Pocket speech model management, server discovery progress display, help content, and general app preferences. It manages complex state through dedicated ViewModels for Chatterbox and KyutaiPocket settings, tracking model download states (not downloaded, downloading, available, loaded, loading, error) and server connection states (not configured, checking, connected, failed). It issues an outbound HTTPS call to unamentis.org to load the privacy policy and exposes the full server discovery tier flow in its UI. It is the control plane through which users configure every aspect of the AI pipeline.

TodoList provides an in-app task management surface where learners track learning targets, reinforcement items, curriculum goals, topic objectives, modules, and auto-resume items. Items move through a four-state lifecycle (pending, inProgress, completed, archived) and are filtered by three views (active, completed, archived). The module includes a full MVVM stack: TodoListViewModel manages state, AddTodoSheet handles creation with type and color selection, TodoItemDetailView presents full item detail, TodoItemRow renders list cells, and TodoHelpSheet provides contextual help. Six item types are color-coded with six named colors (blue, purple, indigo, orange, yellow, green).

UnaMentisTests is the primary test target for the UnaMentis iOS application, containing mock service infrastructure used across the test suite and a focused set of WatchConnectivity session state tests. It imports the main UnaMentis module to access production types and provides MockServices helpers consumed by other test modules. With 12 unit tests across 210 lines it covers a narrow but important slice of the application centered on watch session state transitions. It is the root test executable that XCTest discovers and runs in CI.

The Conformance module contains a suite of contract tests that verify each UnaMentis study module satisfies the shared module interface protocol at both the umCore and umVoice integration levels. It covers Aural Skills, Knowledge Bowl, Oral Exam, Quiz Bowl, SAT Prep, and a Template module, using a shared ModuleConformanceSuite harness to run 18 unit tests across 6 files. These tests act as a regression gate ensuring that adding or modifying a module does not silently break the protocol contract that the app shell depends on. They are the closest thing to cross-module integration safety the test suite currently provides.

ModuleTestHarness is a test support library that provides scripted voice session hosting for integration tests. ScriptedModuleHost wires up the UnaMentis module under test with a controlled environment, ScriptedVoiceSession drives a predefined conversation script through the session pipeline, RecordingControlPlane manages the start/stop lifecycle of test recordings, and RecordingTelemetry captures timing and event data during test execution. It imports the UnaMentis production module directly, making it a white-box integration test harness. With one outbound import edge to the main app target, it bridges the test and production targets.

The Integration module contains 54 integration tests spanning the full audio pipeline of the UnaMentis app, covering barge-in coordinator routing, barge-in latency measurement, GLM ASR inference, live inference end-to-end paths, Pocket TTS synthesis, session engine state transitions, and voice session orchestration. It also includes a KBAudioTestHarness for Knowledge Bowl audio path validation. These tests exercise real component interactions rather than mocks, validating that the AI voice pipeline functions correctly across its critical paths. At 1864 lines across 8 files it is the most substantive test module in the project by a significant margin.

The KnowledgeBowl integration module contains 24 integration tests that validate the Knowledge Bowl answer validation logic and full session lifecycle against real production code. It imports the main UnaMentis target and exercises actual KBSession and answer-checking implementations rather than mocks. The two test files cover answer validation edge cases and session state progression from start through completion. These tests provide the most meaningful coverage of the KB domain engine's runtime behavior anywhere in the test suite.

This is the top-level unit test target for the UnaMentis iOS app, containing 39 test files that cover a broad surface of production code not organized into a named sub-module. Files include tests for APIKeyManager, AnalyticsViewModel, AudioCache, AudioEngine, AudioPlaybackOrchestrator, and BargeIn detection and classification. It imports the main UnaMentis module directly and also references the telemetry endpoint via HTTP to test the MetricsUploadService in its own context. With 524 unit tests running under XCTest in CI, it acts as the quality gate for a large cross-cutting set of production behaviors. The cost-calculation rules it exercises pin expected LLM pricing at $2.50 per million input tokens and $10.00 per million output tokens.

This sub-module holds unit tests for the audio engine configuration, audio segment cache, and playback orchestrator configuration in the UnaMentis app. It receives inbound edges from both the parent Unit module and the Config test module, the latter referencing a self-hosted audio transcription HTTP endpoint in its server config manager tests. The 38 unit tests cover configuration value validation, cache hit and eviction behavior, and orchestrator setup parameters. These tests guard against regressions in the audio pipeline infrastructure that would break voice-driven sessions.

This sub-module contains unit tests for the configuration and API key management subsystem of UnaMentis, covering Keychain storage of API keys, key validation rules, LLM provider info models, server config manager state, and server config model parsing. It references a self-hosted audio transcription endpoint (http://10.0.0.6:11401/v1/audio/transcriptions) in ServerConfigManagerTests, creating an inferred HTTP edge to the audio test module that verifies endpoint construction logic. The cost-estimation rules exercised here pin synthetic usage formulas used to validate cost projection logic (200 input tokens per minute, 150 output tokens per minute, 250 TTS characters per minute, 0.5 speech minutes per minute). Correctness here is important because misconfigured API keys or server endpoints would silently break all LLM and STT service calls.

This sub-module tests the contextual awareness layer of UnaMentis, covering buffer models, confidence monitoring, context expansion tooling, context summarization, and two field-of-view (FOV) context managers for general and reading sessions. The 154 unit tests validate how the app captures, scores, and summarizes what the user is currently looking at or reading in order to feed relevant context to the LLM. ConfidenceMonitorTests verify that the system correctly tracks certainty levels about the current context, while ContextSummarizerTests ensure that long context histories are compressed accurately before being sent to the LLM. This layer sits between raw sensor input and the LLM prompt, and its correctness directly affects the quality of AI-generated responses.

This sub-module tests the curriculum engine, data models, service layer, progress tracker, UMCF (UnaMentis Curriculum Format) parser, and visual asset cache for the structured learning path system. The 105 unit tests validate that curriculum sessions are created correctly, progress statistics are accumulated accurately, imported UMCF files are parsed into the expected model structure, and visual assets are cached and retrieved without data loss. ProgressTrackerStatisticsTests pin statistical calculations such as correct/incorrect ratios and streak lengths that drive adaptive difficulty logic. Without a correct curriculum engine, the app cannot sequence learning content or track student advancement.

This sub-module tests the server discovery subsystem, which allows the UnaMentis iOS client to find and connect to self-hosted LLM and speech servers on the local network. The 57 tests cover CachedServerDiscovery (persistence of previously discovered servers), DeviceDiscoveryManager (orchestration of the discovery process), DiscoveredServer model equality and encoding, and DiscoveryTier priority ordering. Correct discovery behavior is essential for users who run their own Whisper or LLM instances at home; a regression here would cause the app to silently fail to connect to a user-configured server. The tier system implies a fallback chain from preferred to lower-priority servers, and its ordering logic is directly tested.

This sub-module contains the unit test suite for the KnowledgeBowl feature, UnaMentis's competitive trivia and academic quiz mode. With 480 unit tests across 22 test files it is one of the two largest test groups in the project, covering analytics, conference management, domain assignment, domain mix weighting, local pack storage, and golden-parity regression matrices. Domain weighting rules (KBDomain.allCases weight summation) are exercised repeatedly, pinning the invariant that all domain weights must sum to a fixed total. Two time limit configurations are verified: a 1-minute sprint (60 seconds) and a 5-minute standard round (300 seconds). KBGoldenParityMatrix provides a reference fixture for regression testing question scoring parity across releases.

This nested sub-module tests the answer validation layer for KnowledgeBowl, which must determine whether a student's spoken or typed answer matches the correct answer despite phonetic variation, synonyms, word order differences, and partial matches. The 250 unit tests cover five distinct matchers: linguistic (lemma and morphology via NaturalLanguage), n-gram overlap, phonetic (Soundex/Metaphone-style encoding), synonym dictionary lookup, and token-level matching. The breadth of matchers reflects that spoken quiz answers rarely match verbatim, and false negatives (marking a correct answer wrong) are highly disruptive to the user experience. These tests guard a critical correctness boundary in the KnowledgeBowl answer evaluation flow.

This sub-module tests the LLM service layer, which abstracts over multiple AI providers including Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, and self-hosted models. The 89 tests cover streaming and non-streaming response handling, fallback chain behavior (FallbackLLMServiceChain), per-provider cost calculations, and LLM type definitions. Streaming tests for Anthropic and OpenAI verify that chunked server-sent-event responses are assembled correctly into complete AI turns without data loss or ordering errors. The fallback chain tests ensure that when a primary provider fails, the next provider in the configured chain is tried automatically. Correctness here matters because all AI responses in the app flow through this layer.

This sub-module tests the pluggable learning module system of UnaMentis, including AuralSkillsModule (pitch and interval recognition), ContentStoreService (module content retrieval), DrillEngine (question sequencing and scoring), LLMRubricEvaluator (AI-graded open-ended answers), ModuleCatalog, ModuleProtocol conformance, and ModuleTelemetryService. The 213 tests verify that audio signal generation for aural skills uses correct sample-rate-relative frame counts (noteFrames = 0.75 * sampleRate, gapFrames = 0.15 * 0.75 * sampleRate) and that drill engine events (answerWindowOpened, evaluated, itemSkipped, streakChanged, roundEnded) fire in the correct order. The LLMRubricEvaluator tests confirm that free-response evaluation is delegated to the LLM with properly structured rubric prompts. This suite guards the extensible module architecture that underpins all learning modes in the app.

This sub-module tests the QuizBowl engine, metrics collection, and pack management for UnaMentis's rapid-fire quiz format, which is distinct from the more structured KnowledgeBowl mode. The 19 unit tests cover engine lifecycle (question serving, answer evaluation, round termination), metrics accumulation (correct count, response time, streak length), and quiz pack structure validation. Though small relative to other test groups, it guards the correctness of a core engagement feature. The QuizBowl pack format is tested separately from KnowledgeBowl packs, confirming these are distinct content schemas with different field requirements.

This sub-module tests the ReadingList feature, which allows users to manage a personal reading queue within UnaMentis. The 50 unit tests cover two concerns: ReadingListManagerTests for CRUD operations on the reading list (add, remove, reorder, persist) and ReadingListManagerImportTests for bulk importing content from external sources. A correct reading list manager is important because reading sessions are a primary usage mode for the app, feeding text content into the AI reading-assistance pipeline. Import correctness is especially critical because a failed import could silently drop articles from the user's queue without any visible error.

This sub-module tests the ReadingPlayback system, which coordinates AI-voiced narration of reading list content. The 69 tests cover ReadingAudioPreGenerator (pre-computing TTS audio for upcoming paragraphs), ReadingPlaybackService (orchestrating play, pause, skip, and seek), and ReadingPlaybackServiceCoordination (multi-component state synchronization during playback). Pre-generation tests verify that audio is prepared before the user reaches a given paragraph, which is key to eliminating perceived TTS latency during reading. Coordination tests validate that pausing reading also suspends metrics collection and that seeking to a new position correctly resets the pre-generator window.

This sub-module tests the LLM request routing layer, which selects which AI endpoint handles a given task based on task type, conditions, and a configurable routing table. The 119 unit tests cover LLMEndpoint model validation, LLMTaskType classification, PatchPanelService (the runtime router that applies routing rules), RoutingCondition logic evaluation, and RoutingTable configuration parsing. The suite references OpenAI as an external service, confirming that endpoint tests include OpenAI-compatible API URLs as valid routing targets alongside self-hosted and other cloud providers. Correct routing is important because sending the wrong task type to the wrong provider can produce poor results or incur unnecessary cost.

This sub-module tests cross-cutting app services, with a strong focus on the GLMASR on-device speech recognition pipeline. The 162 unit tests cover FeatureFlagService, GLMASROnDeviceProvider (GGUF model loading and inference), GLMASROnDeviceConfiguration, GLMASRSTTService, GLMASRAudioProcessing (sample windowing and VAD threshold calculation), GLMASRHealthMonitor, GLMASRUnifiedGGUF, and STTProviderRouter. Audio processing rules pin threshold frames at Int(sampleRate * thresholdSeconds) and maximum buffer size at sampleRate * 30 samples (30 seconds of audio). Model error handling tests verify the .modelNotFound and .modelLoadFailed error cases that determine whether the on-device STT path is available or must fall back to cloud transcription.

This nested sub-module tests voice-specific service behaviors including VoiceBookmarkService and VoiceCommandRecognizer. The 58 unit tests verify that users can set and retrieve audio position bookmarks via voice commands, and that the recognizer correctly parses spoken directives such as 'bookmark this' or 'go back'. These services bridge raw STT output and high-level app navigation, so recognition failures would silently drop user intents during hands-free operation. The VoiceBookmarkService interacts with the reading playback position system, making its correctness a dependency for hands-free reading workflows.

This sub-module tests the SessionManager state machine and turn lifecycle that live in the production UnaMentis/Core/Session module, which carries no test files of its own. The 52 unit tests cover SessionConfig validation, individual chat turn handling including timing and attribution, full state machine transitions (SessionManagerStateMachineTests), and the complete turn lifecycle from user speech detected to AI response delivered (SessionManagerTurnLifecycleTests). These tests are the primary quality gate for the production session orchestrator. A regression in session state transitions would break every AI conversation in the app.

This sub-module tests the speech-to-text abstraction layer, which presents a unified STT interface over multiple providers including on-device and cloud backends. The 31 unit tests cover audio format conversion (STTAudioConversionTests), the STT error taxonomy (STTErrorTests), and provider capability declarations (STTProviderTests). Audio conversion tests are critical because the app's audio engine may produce PCM at different sample rates or bit depths than a given STT provider expects, and silent format mismatches produce garbled transcriptions. The provider tests verify that each STT backend correctly declares its supported audio formats and latency tier.

This sub-module tests the telemetry and metrics infrastructure that tracks app-side performance and usage signals. It receives inbound edges from both the production Session module (which uploads metrics via HTTP to a telemetry endpoint) and the parent Unit test module (which also exercises MetricsUploadService), making it a shared verification target for the upload pipeline. The 91 unit tests cover DeviceMetrics collection, MetricsExporter batching and flushing, MetricsUploadQueue ordering and retry, TTFAInstrumentation (time-to-first-audio latency tracking), and TelemetryEngine rate limiting. Rate limiting tests verify that events beyond a per-minute cap are dropped before being counted, using dynamic event topic names (t-\(index) and topic-\(index)) to generate high-volume event streams.

This sub-module tests the To-do item management system in UnaMentis, which allows the AI to create and manage task items on the user's behalf during sessions. The 114 unit tests cover TodoItem source attribution (tracking which AI tool or user action created each item), status lifecycle (open, in-progress, completed, dismissed), type classification (task, reminder, follow-up), and TodoManager CRUD operations and persistence. Source attribution tests are notable because the app's AI can autonomously create to-do items, and correct attribution is needed for the user to understand which items were generated by AI versus manually entered. The manager tests verify that persistence round-trips preserve all item state without data loss.

This sub-module tests the LLM tool-call system, which allows the AI to invoke structured tools (such as todo creation and web search) during a conversation turn. The 57 unit tests cover LLMToolService (tool registration and dispatch), TodoToolHandler (executing todo-related tool calls), ToolCallProcessorContext (accumulated state during multi-step tool call processing), ToolCallProcessor (the main execution loop), and WebSearchToolHandler (invoking web search from AI tool calls). Correct tool call processing is important because a malformed tool call that silently succeeds with wrong arguments would cause the AI to take incorrect actions on the user's behalf. The WebSearch handler tests ensure search queries extracted from LLM output are forwarded with the correct structure.

This sub-module tests the text-to-speech abstraction layer, covering on-device model configuration, audio chunk handling, provider capability declarations, voice configuration, and pronunciation preprocessing. The 69 unit tests verify ChatterboxConfig parameters for the on-device TTS model, audio chunk assembly from streamed TTS output, provider capability records, voice selection and configuration validation, and PronunciationProcessor text transformations that expand abbreviations and normalize numbers and symbols before synthesis. Pronunciation preprocessing tests are particularly important because incorrect text normalization produces audibly wrong speech, which is immediately noticeable in a voice-first app.

This sub-module tests the view model layer for several user-facing screens in UnaMentis, including settings screens for on-device TTS (Chatterbox) and ASR (KyutaiPocket), a developer debug conversation view, the reading list screen, the reading playback controls, and the to-do list. The 76 unit tests verify that user actions produce the correct published state changes, that async data loading results are surfaced correctly to the view, and that settings persist after the view model is reinitialized from stored state. These tests guard the presentation logic that drives the app's primary UI surfaces without requiring a running SwiftUI view hierarchy.

name: WatchModuleCatalog.swift
text: UnaMentis - Watch Module Catalog (Shared) The single source of truth for modules reachable on the watch surface. Why this exists (a Phase 1 decision, see MODULE_SDK_SPEC.md sections 8 and 13): the full iOS ModuleCatalog lives under UnaMentis/Core/Modules, which is NOT a source of the watchOS target (project.yml gives the watch target only `UnaMentis Watch App/` and `Shared/`). The iOS ModuleManifest also pulls in iOS-only host machinery. So the watch cannot import ModuleCatalog directly. Rather than hardcode a KB reference at the watch presentation site, the watch resolves its modules through this catalog. It is deliberately lightweight: per-module identity plus a root-view factory, one entry per watch-capable module. This file lives in Shared so the module identity list has one home reachable from both targets. The root-view factory references watch-only views, so the whole entry list is compiled only on watchOS; the iOS build sees the same identities via `moduleIds` without the watch views. When the SDK's cross-platform manifest sharing lands (spec Phase 7), this merges with the unified catalog. Until then this is the smallest correct way to make the watch route catalog-driven instead of hardcoded.

name: BargeInClassifier.swift
text: UnaMentis - Barge-In Classifier ================================ The single decision point for "what kind of barge-in is this?" When the user interrupts the AI (a confirmed barge-in), the transcript is either an explicit COMMAND (bookmark, next, repeat, ...) or the user ENGAGING the material (a question, a comment, a request for explanation). Those two cases route to completely different handling: a command executes locally and silently, an engagement opens a conversational turn with the LLM. Before this type existed the two paths were split and never unified: VoiceCommandRecognizer was used only inside Knowledge Bowl, and ResponseIntent.classify was used only to pick a filler clip. Nothing decided command-vs-engagement for a barge-in. This is that decision, in one place, so every narrating surface routes barge-ins the same way and so the decision can be measured against a labeled corpus (see BargeInMeasurementHarness). Policy (v1, deliberately simple so it is measurable then tuned): 1. Run the local command recognizer. If it returns a result that meets the execution threshold (confidence >= 0.75), the barge-in is a command. 2. Otherwise it is an engagement, sub-typed by ResponseIntent for filler. The command vocabulary overlaps engagement language ("again", "go back", "wait"), so this baseline will misclassify some cases. That error rate is exactly what the measurement quantifies; thresholds and phrases are then tuned against real numbers rather than guesses.

name: BargeInCoordinator.swift
text: UnaMentis - Barge-In Coordinator ================================ THE single barge-in pipeline that every narrating surface plugs into. The mandate: anywhere the app speaks to the user, the user can barge in, and the same gate decides what to do with the sound -> a known COMMAND, or a CONVERSATIONAL interruption answered by interactive AI. Reader, assistant, chat, learning all use this exact pipeline (the available commands may differ per surface). Modules opt in case-by-case (you don't barge in on an active quiz), simply by choosing whether to create a coordinator. One audio stream in, two outcomes out: VAD detect (BargeInDetector) -> capture the utterance -> classify (BargeInClassifier, via BargeInResponder) -> command? execute it. -> conversation? answer it (LLM+TTS). The surface supplies its AudioEngine (VAD + transcript via attachSTT), its valid commands, its LLM/TTS, and a thin delegate for pause/resume/execute/play.

name: BargeInDetector.swift
text: UnaMentis - Barge-In Detector ============================= The single detection pipeline for barge-in across every narrating surface (session, reader, curriculum, Knowledge Bowl). This actor owns ONLY the detection decision; it performs no audio side effects, no telemetry, no UI. It emits timestamped `BargeInEvent` values and lets the consumer decide. CORE INVARIANT (the product principle): ongoing narration must be very hard to interrupt. Constantly listening for a barge-in must NOT disrupt the flow. Background noise, music, or the AI's own voice echoing into the mic must never stop narration. Only a GENUINE barge-in interrupts, and "genuine" means SUSTAINED speech, not a frame or two above threshold. A brief blip that does not sustain is a false positive: the detector resumes and narration continues seamlessly. State machine: listening --(speech above threshold)--------------> tentative (EVALUATING; consumer keeps narrating) tentative --(speech sustains >= sustainedSpeechMs)-> confirmed (genuine barge; consumer interrupts) tentative --(silence gap > maxGapMs before sustain)-> resumed (false positive; keep narrating) tentative --(safety window elapses with no resolve)-> resumed (backstop; never stuck in tentative) Timing is driven by `VADResult.timestamp` (wall-clock at frame capture, which tracks audio time under the real-time mic delivery the app always uses). This makes the "sustained speech" decision deterministic and unit-testable without real-time sleeps: feed frames with controlled timestamps, read the events.

name: BargeInResponder.swift
text: UnaMentis - Barge-In Responder ============================== The single shared conversational barge-in layer. Every narrating surface (session conversation, direct-streaming lecture, reading list, ...) detects a barge-in the same way (BargeInDetector), transcribes the interrupting utterance, then hands the transcript here. This component classifies it once (BargeInClassifier) and runs the one engagement-response loop: lead with a filler, stream the LLM answer, speak it via TTS, then hand control back to the surface to resume narration. Surface-specific actions (execute a command, pause/resume narration, play an audio chunk through this surface's engine/player) are delegated, so there is exactly one conversational loop and N thin surface adapters, instead of a bespoke loop per surface. The responder is STT-free on purpose: transcription is surface- and environment-specific (and the on-device recognizer differs by surface), so the surface transcribes and passes the text in.

name: ConformanceDrivable.swift
text: UnaMentis - Conformance Drivability The headless-driving seam the UM-Voice conformance suite drives modules through. MODULE_SDK_SPEC.md section 9 requires that "every activity marked voice-first completes with zero touch events". The spec does not, however, name the API a conformance harness uses to run a module's voice activity without SwiftUI. This protocol is that API: a small, UI-free entry point a module adopts so its primary voice-first activity can run driven ONLY by a host VoiceSession (the scripted one in tests, the real unified pipeline in production). Design (ratified deviation, tracked for the RFC process, see docs/ios/MODULE_AUTHORING.md and the Phase 6 RFC): - The spec's audio-only surface (section 8) is "not a view surface"; a module declaring it "commits that its voice-first activities run to completion with the screen locked, driven entirely by VoiceSession". `ConformanceDrivable` makes that commitment executable: the same code path the audio-only surface uses in production is the one conformance drives. - The activity receives an already-acquired VoiceSession. The HOST owns acquisition and release (section 5.1 exclusivity); the module never instantiates audio. This keeps the "one voice pipeline" invariant (goal 3) true even in the headless path. - The activity returns a `ConformanceRunResult` the suite asserts on: whether the primary activity reached completion, how many attempts it evaluated, and the module-scoped voice states it exercised (so command-vocabulary checks have something concrete to inspect).

name: DrillEngine.swift
text: UnaMentis - Drill Engine MODULE_SDK_SPEC.md section 6.3, engine "drill/1" The generic, descriptor-driven rapid-practice state machine. One engine, many formats: SAT vocabulary and mental-math drills are both expressed as data (DrillFormatDescriptor) plus a content pack, not code. This engine is also the intended substrate for Aural Skills and future flash-card packs (section 6.3 calls drill "the primary watch engine"), so it is deliberately kept lean and content-agnostic. Boundaries, deliberate (mirroring QuizMatchEngine's contract, section 6.1): - ZERO knowledge of any specific module. Items arrive through a provider closure carrying host EvaluationSpecs; modules adapt to the engine, never the reverse. The provider also owns SCHEDULING: the module orders items per the descriptor policy (free = pack order/shuffled, review = ascending mastery, via DrillScheduling below) before handing the list over, so the engine reads no ProgressStore itself and stays trivially testable. - UI-agnostic. The engine emits DrillEvents on an AsyncStream (single consumer) and exposes command methods; a module view model renders events and forwards user intents (spoken or typed). - The engine does not own the voice pipeline. The module acquires the exclusive VoiceSession (with descriptor-derived endpointing via `DrillFormatDescriptor.voicePipelineConfig`) and hands it to `start(voice:)`; the module remains responsible for release. - Progress and telemetry are emitted per evaluated answer through the injected DrillHostContext (AttemptRecord + mastery observation + module.attempt), exactly the writes the SDK spec requires (sections 5.4 and 5.6). - Answer capture supports BOTH the spoken path (listen, then submit the transcript) and a text path (submitAnswer directly), so a non-voice UI (the on-screen math keypad) drives the same evaluation and recording code.

name: DrillFormatDescriptor.swift
text: UnaMentis - Drill Format Descriptor MODULE_SDK_SPEC.md section 6.3, schema "format-descriptor.drill/1" A drill format descriptor is DATA: the complete parameterization of one rapid item-practice session, consumed by the generic DrillEngine. New drill formats (a vocabulary drill, a mental-math drill, a future flash-card or aural-skills pack) should require no new engine code, only a new descriptor plus a content pack. Spec section 6.3 is a one-paragraph sketch ("Descriptor selects item types, session shapes (count, time-boxed, streak), scheduling policy (scheduler-driven review vs free practice), and watch suitability per item type"). This is the concrete Codable form of that sketch, following the QuizMatchFormatDescriptor precedent (section 6.1). The frictions this surfaces against the sketch are filed for the RFC process (docs/modules/rfcs/, and the final report): - The sketch names no oral-block equivalent, but a voice-driven drill needs answer endpointing (silence threshold, max utterance) exactly as the quiz-match `oral` block does (RFC 0005 item 1's precedent). Added here as an optional `voice` block reusing the same field names. - `itemTypes` is a list of schema-qualified item-type names the format accepts (e.g. "drill-items/1"); the sketch says "item types" without shape. - `sessionShapes` is a list (count and/or time-boxed) rather than a single value, so one format can offer several session lengths. A session picks one. Per the versioning policy (section 10), unknown JSON fields are tolerated and every field beyond the identity core is optional or defaulted.

name: DrillModels.swift
text: UnaMentis - Drill Engine Models MODULE_SDK_SPEC.md section 6.3, engine "drill/1" The value types the DrillEngine consumes and emits. All are module-agnostic: the engine has zero knowledge of SAT Prep, Aural Skills, or any future flash-card module. Modules adapt their pack content onto `DrillItem` (carrying a host `EvaluationSpec` and a skill tag) and render `DrillEvent`s however their UI wants. This mirrors the QuizMatchEngine models (section 6.1) so the two engines stay shaped alike.

name: ExaminerBrain.swift
text: UnaMentis - Examiner Brain MODULE_SDK_SPEC.md section 6.2: the adaptive-questioning seam. The OralExamEngine owns the stage state machine; WHAT the examiner asks and HOW rubric scores are produced is delegated to an injected ExaminerBrain. This keeps the engine deterministic and headless-testable, and it keeps LLM routing out of engine code entirely: the production brain (module-side) rides the app's LLM policy, tests inject a scripted brain, and the rule-based brain below is the offline Tier 0 floor. Grounding requirement (ORAL_EXAM_STUDIO_MODULE_SPEC.md section 4): follow-up questions must derive from the syllabus item, the exam's question pool, and the learner's own words. Generic questions are a defect. Every brain receives the full ExaminerContext so it has no excuse.

name: OralExamDeliveryMetrics.swift
text: UnaMentis - Oral Exam Delivery Metrics MODULE_SDK_SPEC.md section 6.2: evaluation.deliveryMetrics ("pace", "fillerWords", "hesitations"). Delivery metrics come from transcript timing analysis, not the LLM (ORAL_EXAM_STUDIO_MODULE_SPEC.md section 4). The analyzer is a pure value computation over captured utterance segments so its math is unit-testable without any audio: the engine records wall-clock timing around each `listen` call and hands the segments here. Timing model, stated so the numbers mean something: - A segment's duration spans listen start to listen return. A segment that ended on the silence threshold therefore INCLUDES that trailing silence, which the analyzer subtracts to approximate actual speaking time. - Each silence-ended segment that is followed by another segment in the same monologue is one hesitation gap: the learner went quiet long enough for the endpointer to fire, then resumed. Finer-grained intra-utterance gap timing needs per-word timestamps the pipeline does not surface yet (candidate RFC once STT word timing is exposed).

name: OralExamEngine.swift
text: UnaMentis - Oral Exam Engine MODULE_SDK_SPEC.md section 6.2, engine "oral-exam/1" The generic, descriptor-driven oral examination state machine: timed preparation, timed presentation (long-form monologue capture), adaptive questioning grounded in the syllabus item and the learner's own words, and rubric feedback. One engine, many exam formats: Grand Oral, Maturita, Matura, and interview formats are data (OralExamFormatDescriptor), not code. Boundaries, deliberate (the QuizMatchEngine pattern): - ZERO knowledge of any specific module. Topics arrive as OralExamTopic values; modules adapt their pack items to the engine, never the reverse. - UI-agnostic. The engine emits OralExamEvents on an AsyncStream (single consumer) and exposes command methods; a module view model renders events and forwards user intents (taps and voice commands). - The engine does not own the voice pipeline. The module acquires the exclusive VoiceSession (with descriptor-derived long-form endpointing via `OralExamFormatDescriptor.voicePipelineConfig`) and hands it to `start(voice:)`; the module remains responsible for release. The engine does not consume `voice.events` (single-consumer stream): partial transcripts and recognized commands stay with the module, which calls engine commands (endStage/skipQuestion/pause/stop). - Question generation and rubric scoring are delegated to the injected ExaminerBrain; the engine computes delivery metrics itself from transcript timing (OralExamDeliveryAnalyzer) because the module spec says the LLM never produces them. - Progress and telemetry are emitted per answered examiner question through the injected OralExamHostContext (AttemptRecord + module.attempt), plus one rubric-driven mastery observation at feedback time. Note on attempt semantics: an oral exchange has no correct/incorrect verdict, so an answered question records `correct: true` (participation) and mastery carries the actual quality signal (average rubric score). Spec 6.2 is silent on attempt sema

name: QuizMatchEngine.swift
text: UnaMentis - Quiz Match Engine MODULE_SDK_SPEC.md section 6.1, engine "quiz-match/1" The generic, descriptor-driven quiz match state machine, extracted from Knowledge Bowl's oral practice flow (migration Phase 5). One engine, many formats: Knowledge Bowl's team-buzz short-form practice and Quiz Bowl's individual-buzz pyramidal tossup/bonus play are both expressed as data (QuizMatchFormatDescriptor), not code. Boundaries, deliberate: - ZERO knowledge of any specific module. Questions arrive through a provider closure carrying host EvaluationSpecs; modules adapt to the engine, never the reverse. - UI-agnostic. The engine emits QuizMatchEvents on an AsyncStream (single consumer) and exposes command methods; a module view model renders events and forwards user intents. - The engine does not own the voice pipeline. The module acquires the exclusive VoiceSession (with descriptor-derived endpointing via `QuizMatchFormatDescriptor.voicePipelineConfig`) and hands it to `start(voice:)`; the module remains responsible for release. The engine also does not consume `voice.events`: partial transcripts stay with the module (single-consumer stream), and the buzz fast path is still a host stub (RFC 0002 item 4), so buzzes arrive via the `buzz(atCharacterIndex:)` command. - Progress and telemetry are emitted per evaluated answer through the injected QuizMatchHostContext (AttemptRecord + mastery observation + module.attempt), exactly the writes the KB view model previously made. Session-level registration (watch control plane) stays with the module, which calls pause/resume/stop here from its registered-session callbacks. Scope (Phase 5): the flow KB oral practice exercises today, plus the descriptor-driven mechanics the Quiz Bowl skeleton proves (pyramidal power scoring, interrupt negs, multi-part bonuses, a minimal rebound hook). Design notes: - Fields tolerate unknown values where the spec says so (capabilities is an open, namespaced set; unknown names are permitted and ignored). - Adding optional fields within a major spec version is non-breaking (section 10.2, additive-only schemas).

name: ModuleProtocol.swift
text: UnaMentis - Module Protocol Defines the interface for specialized training modules Modules are self-contained training systems that can be registered and discovered by the app. Each module provides its own views, session management, and progress tracking. This protocol is evolving toward the spec's `UnaMentisModule` contract (MODULE_SDK_SPEC.md section 4) without breaking existing modules. A module now declares a `ModuleManifest` (the single source of metadata truth) and gains async lifecycle hooks. The legacy display properties are derived from the manifest via a protocol extension, so metadata lives in one place.

name: ModuleRegistry.swift

name: ModuleService.swift

name: ContentStoreService.swift
text: UnaMentis - Content Store Host Service MODULE_SDK_SPEC.md section 5.3, capability "content.canonical-question/1" The host-owned content layer. Modules never read raw bundle files or manage their own download caches: they query for packs, pull typed items out of a pack, import packs from a URL (coach/AirDrop distribution), and download packs from the server. Pack integrity (sha256) and schema compatibility are the store's job (section 5.3): a corrupt or mismatched pack is refused with a user-visible error, never loaded silently. Phase 3 scope is what Knowledge Bowl exercises: the bundled kb-sample-questions.json is exposed as pack id "kb-sample-questions"; importPack parses and integrity-checks a PackManifest (section 7); download wires to the existing ModuleService/ModuleRegistry server path. The canonical question transformer layer (section 5.3) is a later phase.

name: DefaultResponseEvaluationService.swift
text: UnaMentis - Default Response Evaluation Service MODULE_SDK_SPEC.md section 5.2. The production evaluator. It reproduces Knowledge Bowl's algorithmic answer validation, generalized off KB types: category-aware normalization, the exact/acceptable/Levenshtein baseline, and the enhanced tiers (synonyms, Double Metaphone, n-gram, token, linguistic) gated by the spec's named strictness profile. The tables of synonyms come from the profile, not the evaluator (EvaluationSynonyms). llmRubric ships via the injected LLMRubricEvaluating seam (structured rubric scoring over the app's LLM routing policy; the Oral Exam engine's feedback path). semantic remains declared but NOT advertised: the KB embeddings tier was never wired into a live call site, so there is no implemented, testable tier to lift; it lights up once the host manages shared embedding assets (section 5.2). pitchRhythm is reserved.

name: EvaluationMatchers.swift
text: UnaMentis - Evaluation Matchers MODULE_SDK_SPEC.md section 5.2 (eval.text-fuzzy/1). The algorithmic fuzzy-matching stack, MOVED from Knowledge Bowl's Services/KnowledgeBowl/Algorithms into the host evaluation service and generalized to carry no KB types. These are the exact algorithms the KB validator used (Double Metaphone phonetics, character/word n-gram similarity, token Jaccard/Dice similarity, and Apple NaturalLanguage lemmatization), so the lift is behavior-preserving. They are stateless value types, safe to hold inside the actor-backed evaluation service.

name: EvaluationNormalization.swift
text: UnaMentis - Evaluation Normalization MODULE_SDK_SPEC.md section 5.2. Category-aware answer normalization, MOVED from KBAnswerValidator and generalized from KBAnswerType to AnswerCategory. The behavior is identical to KB's normalize/normalizeText/normalizePerson/... family so the lift preserves verdicts. Punctuation stripping, article removal, "Last, First" reordering, title/subtitle handling, written-number parsing, place abbreviations, and scientific-formula whitespace removal all match the legacy validator.

name: EvaluationSynonyms.swift
text: UnaMentis - Evaluation Synonym Resource MODULE_SDK_SPEC.md section 5.2 / 5.7. Domain synonym data supplied to the fuzzy evaluator by a strictness profile. This is the generalization of Knowledge Bowl's KBSynonymDictionaries / KBSynonymMatcher: the synonym tables are no longer baked into the evaluator, they are profile-supplied data. The knowledge-bowl bundle below reproduces KB's dictionaries verbatim so the lift is behavior-preserving; other modules (or server-delivered profiles, section 5.7) supply their own.

name: LLMRubricEvaluator.swift
text: UnaMentis - LLM Rubric Evaluator MODULE_SDK_SPEC.md section 5.2, capability "eval.llm-rubric/1" Structured rubric scoring over the app's LLM service abstraction: rubric dimensions plus syllabus context plus the learner's transcript in; per-dimension 0-5 scores, one improvement action per dimension, and a short spoken summary out. This is the evaluation engine behind oral-exam feedback (spec 5.2: "rubric in, per-dimension scores plus spoken-feedback text out"). Routing: the evaluator does NOT hardcode a provider. It resolves an LLMService per call through `ModuleLLMResolver`, which follows the app's existing LLM routing policy (the same provider-selection and fallback priority the session flow uses): the user-selected provider first, then cloud providers with configured API keys, then the self-hosted server, then the on-device model. Tests inject a scripted LLM through the resolver closure (paid-API mock policy: the only LLM mock lives in UnaMentisTests/Helpers/MockServices.swift). Spoken summary budget: the module spec caps spoken feedback at 60 seconds. At a typical 150 words-per-minute TTS rate that is 150 words; the evaluator enforces the cap by truncation so a chatty model cannot blow the budget.

name: ModuleTelemetryService.swift
text: UnaMentis - Module Telemetry Host Service MODULE_SDK_SPEC.md section 5.6, capability "telemetry/1" App-global telemetry with a module dimension. This is the host service that replaces per-module telemetry: modules never instantiate their own TelemetryEngine, they emit through `host.telemetry`, and every event carries the emitting module's ID so cross-module analysis stays possible. The production implementation routes into the app-global `TelemetryEngine` (the same actor that owns session latency, cost, and the error-log drill-down), so module events land in the one place session telemetry already lives. The required taxonomy is small and fixed (section 5.6): module.session.start/end, module.activity.start/end, module.attempt. Free-form module events are also allowed.

name: ProgressStoreService.swift
text: UnaMentis - Progress Store and Unified Proficiency Host Service MODULE_SDK_SPEC.md section 5.4, capabilities "progress/1" and "proficiency/1" The host-owned, module-namespaced persistence layer. Modules never write raw files: they store structured attempts, keep module-private key/value state, and read/write the shared unified proficiency model through this service. All persistence is namespaced by module ID (section 5.4 and 11), which gives every module GDPR export (`exportAll`) and erasure (`deleteAll`) for free. This is the minimal spec-shaped implementation Knowledge Bowl exercises: - AttemptRecord round-trips to a per-module JSON store. - keyValue(namespace:) is a module-private KV store, isolated per module. - proficiency/reportMastery back a simple 0-100 mastery model keyed by StandardDomain, shared across modules. It is file-backed rather than Core Data on purpose: KB stats are already file-backed JSON (KBSessionStore), the data volume is small, and a temp-dir store makes the "real over mock" unit tests trivial. The root directory is injectable so tests run in isolation.

name: ResponseEvaluationService.swift
text: UnaMentis - Response Evaluation Host Service MODULE_SDK_SPEC.md section 5.2, capabilities "eval.*". The platform answer-evaluation service. It generalizes Knowledge Bowl's algorithmic answer validation (exact, acceptable-alternatives, Levenshtein fuzzy, and the enhanced tiers: domain synonyms, Double Metaphone phonetics, n-gram, token, and linguistic matching) into a host service every module can use, with named strictness profiles in place of KB's hardcoded regional strictness. Phase 4 scope (MODULE_SDK_SPEC.md section 13): - textExact, textFuzzy, numeric, and choice evaluators ship and are tested. textFuzzy is the moved KB algorithm stack, generalized to carry no KB types: domain synonyms arrive as a profile-supplied resource, not baked-in. - semantic and llmRubric are DECLARED but advertised unavailable: the KB embeddings/LLM tiers are never wired into the live call site (the oral session constructs the validator with no embeddings/LLM service), so there is no implemented, testable tier to lift. When those land as host-managed shared model assets they light up behind these kinds. - pitchRhythm is reserved (section 5.2) and always unavailable.

name: SessionRegistrationService.swift
text: UnaMentis - Session Registration Host Service MODULE_SDK_SPEC.md section 5.9, capability "session.registration/1" Module sessions register as first-class app sessions. One contract closes three gaps at once (section 5.9): - the Watch control plane (pause/mute/stop, progress) works for module sessions, not just core curriculum sessions; - module sessions appear in the session error-log drill-down; - latency/stability metrics can cover module sessions. The watch hookup uses the exact same mechanism core sessions use (WatchConnectivityService.syncSessionState + setCommandHandler): on begin we install the command handler and push initial state; on update we push new state; on end we clear the handler and push idle. Only one session holds the watch handler at a time, matching the existing single-handler model. The watch plane and error sink are injected behind small protocols so the service is unit-testable without WatchConnectivity or a live TelemetryEngine.

name: ToneGenerationService.swift
text: UnaMentis - Tone Generation Host Service RFC 0007, capability "audio.tonegen/1". Host synthesis of symbolic music prompts (notes, melodic sequences, harmonic stacks, simple progressions) for the Aural Skills module and any future music-adjacent module. This service is PURE SYNTHESIS: it renders PCM and owns no audio hardware, no engine, no player node. Playback happens through the ONE unified pipeline: the rendered `PreRenderedAudio` travels inside an `Utterance` to `VoiceSession.speak`, the exact route Phase 2 built for server-pregenerated question audio (AudioPlaybackOrchestrator over the shared AudioEngine). That keeps the "modules never own audio" mandate true for non-speech audio with zero new playback machinery. Synthesis details: - Equal temperament, A4 = 440 Hz, MIDI note numbering (C4 = 60). - Pure sine timbre in v1 (`ToneTimbre.sine`); richer timbres are additive enum cases per RFC 0007's open questions. - Every event gets a soft cosine attack/release envelope so buffer edges never click, a hard requirement of the RFC. - Rendering is deterministic and side-effect free, so conformance tests run it for real, headlessly.

name: UnifiedVoiceSessionService.swift
text: UnaMentis - Unified Voice Session Service The production VoiceSessionService on the app's single voice pipeline. Composes the EXISTING unified pipeline components, creating no parallel audio machinery: - AudioEngine via AudioEngineCache.shared (one capture/playback pipeline) - AudioPlaybackOrchestrator for TTS playback (bounded synthesis: stalls and empty streams surface as errors, never silent hangs) - the canonical BargeInDetector (the ONE detector; tuned by BargeInTuning) - the shared on-device providers (AppleSpeechSTTService; Pocket TTS with Apple TTS fallback, honoring the user's ttsProvider setting) Exclusive acquisition is arbitrated by VoicePipelineOwnership against the core session (SessionManager) and other module sessions.

name: UtteranceEndpointer.swift
text: UnaMentis - Utterance Endpointer Config-driven utterance endpointing for the VoiceSession host service. This replaces per-module endpointing code (Knowledge Bowl's hand-rolled 1.5 s silence rule) with one policy-driven state machine. Like BargeInDetector, timing is driven by `VADResult.timestamp` so decisions are deterministic and unit-testable without real-time sleeps: feed frames with controlled timestamps, read the decisions. State machine (per listen call): waiting --(speech frame)-------------------------> speaking waiting --(answerTimeout elapses, no speech)------> finalize(.timeout) speaking --(silence >= silenceThreshold)-----------> finalize(.silence) speaking --(duration >= maxUtteranceDuration)------> finalize(.maxUtteranceDuration)

name: VoicePipelineOwnership.swift
text: UnaMentis - Voice Pipeline Ownership The single arbiter for exclusive voice pipeline access. The app has ONE voice pipeline (the unified-voice-pipeline mandate). This actor is the mechanism that keeps it exclusive: a core tutoring session and a module voice session may never capture or play concurrently. Core sessions claim `.coreSession` in SessionManager.startSession and release in stopSession; module sessions claim `.module` through UnifiedVoiceSessionService.acquire and release via VoiceSession.release. Claiming while another holder is active throws VoiceSessionError.pipelineBusy, so conflicts surface as typed errors at the acquisition point instead of as two audio stacks fighting over the mic.

name: VoiceSessionService.swift
text: UnaMentis - VoiceSession Host Service Contract MODULE_SDK_SPEC.md section 5.1, capability "voice.session/1" The single voice pipeline, exposed to modules as a host service. Modules never instantiate STT, TTS, VAD, or audio engines; they acquire a VoiceSession from the host, speak and listen through it, and release it. The production implementation (UnifiedVoiceSessionService) composes the app's existing unified pipeline: AudioEngine, AudioPlaybackOrchestrator, the canonical BargeInDetector, and the shared on-device STT/TTS providers. This file is the contract only; it has no audio dependencies of its own beyond the shared value types it reuses (VADResult, BargeInEvent, CachedSegmentAudio, VoiceCommand).

text: UnaMentis - Metrics Exporter ============================ Exports latency and telemetry metrics to the management server in a unified format compatible with both iOS and web clients. UNIFIED METRIC FORMAT --------------------- This exporter uses the same metric schema as the web client, enabling cross-platform analytics and comparison: ```json { "client": "ios", "clientId": "device-uuid", "sessionId": "session-uuid", "timestamp": "2024-01-01T12:00:00Z", "metrics": { "stt_latency_ms": 150.0, "llm_ttfb_ms": 200.0, "llm_completion_ms": 800.0, "tts_ttfb_ms": 100.0, "tts_completion_ms": 400.0, "e2e_latency_ms": 1250.0 }, "providers": { "stt": "deepgram-nova3", "llm": "anthropic/claude-3-5-haiku", "tts": "chatterbox" }, "resources": { "cpu_percent": 45.2, "memory_mb": 256.0, "thermal_state": "nominal" } } ``` BATCHING & RELIABILITY ---------------------- - Metrics are queued locally if network is unavailable - Batch uploads reduce network overhead - Automatic retry with exponential backoff - Queue persisted to disk for crash recovery SEE ALSO -------- - MetricsUploadService.swift: Session metrics upload - TestResult.swift: Test result data model - server/management/latency_harness_api.py: Server endpoints DEBUG ONLY ---------- This exporter is used exclusively by the debug latency harness hooks and reads device-identifying values (IDFV, device name). name: AuralContentLoader.swift
text: UnaMentis - Aural Skills Content Loader Loads the bundled aural-items/1 starter pack THROUGH the host ContentStore so licensing and integrity enforcement (MODULE_SDK_SPEC.md section 7) apply to this module's content exactly as they do to imported packs. Mechanics: the pack ships in the app bundle as two flat resources (aural-starter-manifest.json, aural-starter-items.json) because the project's resource phase flattens directories. The loader stages them into a temporary pack directory with the canonical names (manifest.json, items.json) and imports through `host.content.importPack(from:)`, which hash-checks the payload before registering it. The decoded entries are then expanded by the deterministic generator into the concrete item list. If the ContentStore import path is unavailable (no imports root, say), the loader falls back to decoding the same bundled payload directly so the Tier 0 drill still works; the fallback is logged, never silent.

name: AuralDrillSession.swift
text: UnaMentis - Aural Skills Drill Session The module's drill loop, factored as a plain async function over host services and a VoiceSession so the SAME code path runs from the SwiftUI session view, the audio-only surface, and the UM-Voice conformance harness (zero touch). This is the ExampleEchoModule pattern with the aural domain: play prompt (host tone generation through the ONE pipeline) -> listen for a spoken label -> evaluate against the module's music profile -> feedback (confirm, or name the answer, replay, coach with solfège) -> record attempt + mastery + telemetry Repeat-on-request is honored both as the unified `repeatLast` command and as a plain spoken "repeat"/"again" transcript.

name: AuralItems.swift
text: UnaMentis - Aural Skills Item Schema (aural-items/1) The module-side content schema per AURAL_SKILLS_MODULE_SPEC.md section 3. Key property of the schema: prompts are SYNTHESIZED, not recorded. Items declare notes/chords symbolically and the host tone generator (RFC 0007, audio.tonegen/1) renders them, so packs are tiny and transposition is free. The pack's items.json is an array of `AuralPackEntry` values, each either a concrete item or a compact template the module's deterministic generator (AuralItemGenerator) expands at load. Templates keep the JSON small while the drill still sees every transposition as a first-class item. The pack JSON remains the source of truth; the generator adds nothing that is not derivable from it plus the fixed music-theory tables.

name: AuralSkillsModule.swift
text: UnaMentis - Aural Skills Trainer Module (Module C) Music ear training per AURAL_SKILLS_MODULE_SPEC.md: interval recognition, triad quality, major/minor discrimination, cadence recognition, and scale-degree solfège, drilled entirely by voice. Prompts are synthesized symbolically through the host tone generator (RFC 0007, audio.tonegen/1) and played through the module's VoiceSession on the unified pipeline. Phase 1 (MVP) scope: spoken-label responses only. Sung responses and rhythm echo arrive with eval.pitch-rhythm/1 (module spec section 5, capability candidate 2), which stays reserved.

name: AuralSkillsViews.swift
text: UnaMentis - Aural Skills Views The phone surface: a dashboard of skill-area cards with mastery rings, and a minimal drill session view.
